title: A Monday morning at Meridian, and the coherence problem
excerpt: A staff engineer returns to twelve pull requests and no reckless act. The scene in Chapter 9 shows why output is no longer the scarce thing.

source.title: Chapter 9 — The AI-Native Organization
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 9 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: On Monday morning, a staff engineer at Meridian opens twelve pull requests, four synthetic eval reports and two security review requests. Nobody did anything wrong. That is the point of the scene in Chapter 9.

Meridian is a company well past casual AI adoption. Over the weekend, engineers launched subagents against backlog items. Product used internal tools to spin up three alternative flows for a new onboarding step. Support found a recurring customer complaint and had an agent draft both a help-center update and a proposed product fix.

A dashboard then showed that an internal automation had quietly touched three systems nobody had discussed together on Friday. Any one of them could be hiding another admin-override regression, the throttle on the wrong path from Chapter 4, now buried under a weekend of green checkmarks.
No reckless act
Read the scene again. Each move is locally defensible. Everyone is productive. The chapter says that is the problem.

Meridian is no longer starved for output. It is starved for coherence. Which changes matter? Which are duplicates? Which artifacts reflect current strategy, and which reflect a private interpretation of it? Which outputs are safe to merge, safe to trial, safe to ignore, or dangerous to trust? Who is responsible for saying so when authorship is half human, half machine, and spread across several functions?

This is where the Software Factory stops being only a repo pattern. Earlier chapters showed a team turning a repo into an environment agents can use. Chapter 9 asks what happens next. Someone has to own the rules. Someone has to decide which patterns become standard. The factory becomes a company problem.
Put the questions in order

The chapter gives an order for the questions. Settle ownership first, because every other question needs someone empowered to answer it. Then ask about strategy fit, which discards whole branches cheaply. Ask about safety-to-merge last. It is the expensive per-artifact check, so run it last and least.

Apply that order to the staff engineer's Monday. Without it, twelve pull requests and two security requests become fourteen separate inspections. With it, the first question is who owns each item. The second removes work that does not fit the current plan. Only the survivors earn the costly review.

The chapter names the cost of skipping this order alignment debt. It builds up when execution fans out faster than shared understanding. It comes due as rework, confusion, or an exhausting burst of manual coordination. The remedy is not to ban private leverage. Move alignment earlier, with shared planning, visible decomposition and common review spaces.
Try it on your own Monday

If your team already runs agents on weekends, do a short exercise. Imagine your next Monday. List what would be waiting for you. For each item, write down three things: who owns it, whether it fits the strategy, and what check would make it safe to merge.
Every blank in that list marks a place where your coherence will break first. Fill the blanks before the weekend.

title: What endures in AI engineering is constrained delegation
excerpt: Frameworks, models and interfaces will keep changing. Chapter 10 argues that one pattern for turning machine capability into dependable work will last.

source.title: Chapter 10 — What Endures
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 10 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Omar Khattab built systems, DSPy among them, across years of model turnover. Chapter 10 reports his verdict: they "fundamentally stayed the same over the years," from text-davinci-002 up to o4-mini. The models underneath were swapped out entirely. The structure stayed.

That fact frames the chapter's question. Agent frameworks multiply. Tool protocols proliferate. New releases reorder yesterday's leaderboard. Interfaces move from chat windows to canvases to copilots to swarms. Some of that is real progress. The chapter calls some of it marketing theater with a GPU budget. So what endures?
The chapter's answer is not a framework, a model family or an orchestration fashion. It is a pattern for turning machine capability into dependable work.
The pattern has a name

The chapter calls it constrained delegation. The machine gets a prepared environment, a clearer representation of intent and a workable slice of context. It gets a runtime that can preserve and expose state. Its authority matches the risk. Human review sits where it matters most.

The chapter also defines the pattern by what it excludes: raw generation, autonomous theater, tool sprawl disguised as capability, infinite context pretending to be memory, and a leaderboard screenshot standing in for product trust.

The chapter says the pattern will outlast today's frameworks and likely today's interface assumptions. The reason is simple. The pattern does not work around weak models. It answers the nature of delegated work itself.
Look past the interface

The visible part of a system is not the stable part. A coding agent does not earn trust with a polished diff view. A realtime voice system does not earn trust with natural speech. The question underneath is the same each time: what must be true around the model for delegated work to deserve trust?

The chapter's answer is the environment. Prepared repositories, specs, validations, retrieval systems, memory layers, runtimes, permissions and review surfaces are not accessories. They are how intelligence becomes situated. What endures, the chapter says, is not prompt cleverness but environment design.

Stronger models did not remove this work. They moved it. The chapter says teams that expected better models to dissolve complexity found it migrating into context assembly, eval design, runtime semantics, authority boundaries and organizational throughput. The model grew more capable. The loop around it grew more consequential.

The chapter also rejects the maximalist story of full autonomy. The most useful systems in the book were rarely the ones with the least human involvement. They were the ones with the clearest handoffs. Autonomy is a variable to tune, not a trophy.
Run the strike-out test
Take the plan for your next AI project. Strike out every model name and product name. Read what remains.

Does the plan still name a prepared environment, explicit intent, bounded authority and focused review? Then it rests on the parts the chapter calls durable. Does nothing remain? Then the plan depends on a moment, and the next release may end it.
Do this on the plan that sits open on your desk today. Rewrite one line that names a product so it names the constraint instead.

title: A week of work toward constrained delegation
excerpt: Chapter 10 closes with five practical steps. Here is how a team can run the diagnostic, set an autonomy dial and name an owner in one week.

source.title: Chapter 10 — What Endures
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 10 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Monday morning, a delegated system misbehaves. Someone suggests a bigger model. Chapter 10 closes with a checklist that starts by stopping that suggestion. Constrained delegation, the chapter says, is built one layer at a time, not declared all at once. Here is a week that builds one layer.
Diagnose before you upgrade

Pick the delegated system that misbehaves right now. Before anyone reaches for a bigger model, name which of six layers failed. The layers are legibility, evals, context, runtime, authority and supervision.

The chapter's logic runs down the chain. A legible workplace without evals is not enough. Evals without good context are not enough. Context without a durable runtime is not enough. Runtime without bounded authority is not enough. Security without usable supervision is not enough.

Hold a thirty-minute review with the people who saw the failure. Go through the six layers in order. Ask of each one: did it hold? Write the answer in one sentence. In the two recurring cases the book followed, the model was rarely the layer that failed. Your case may differ. The exercise makes you check before you spend.
Set the dial in writing

Choose one real workflow. Set its autonomy dial on paper. The chapter takes the dial from Joel Hron, who described treating agency this way: turn it up where the work is reversible and recoverable, turn it down where a wrong move costs something you cannot get back.
Write three lines for that workflow. What may the agent do alone? What needs a human? Why? The chapter's warning is blunt. An undocumented dial is a dial nobody actually set.
Name the owner

Before you ship, write down who is accountable for the system's output. The chapter asks for this before something breaks, not after. If no name comes to mind, nobody holds the responsibility yet. Write the name next to the workflow. This takes five minutes.
Build one thing

Now find the gap that hurts most and build one piece to close it. The chapter offers a menu: a legible repo, a real eval slice, a working set instead of a document dump, a durable runtime, a bounded credential, a control plane, a named owner. Pick one. Scope it to this week. The chapter says "one thing," so resist doing three.
Set a six-month reminder
Put a date in your calendar six months out. On that day, reread the seven "make" lines that end the chapter:
Make the task legible.
Make the standards explicit.
Make the context usable.
Make the runtime durable.
Make authority narrow enough to trust.
Make review proportionate to risk.
Make the organization capable of learning.
The chapter sets the bar for the whole book here. The test is not whether you agreed with it. The test is whether more of those seven lines are true of your system than are true today.
So score yourself today. Mark each line true or false for your system, and save the page. In six months, the comparison will be honest because the first score is on paper.

title: What remains human is responsibility, not typing
excerpt: Chapter 10 argues the lasting human role in AI work is responsibility. A six-month test shows whether you have actually assigned it.

source.title: Chapter 10 — What Endures
source.editorialNote: Written for this blog from Chapter 10 of the book. Ideas and quotations come from that chapter.

children.text: Picture a delegated system six months after launch. Its output turns out to be wrong. The person who wrote the prompt moved to a different team long ago. Who answers for the error?
Chapter 10 uses this scene as a test. If no name comes to mind, the chapter says, the responsibility was never assigned. It evaporated along with the context window that produced the output.
The shallow debate
The test sits inside a larger argument about what remains human. The chapter calls one version of that debate shallow: the version that fixates on which tasks people will keep doing by hand.

Humans may type less. They may implement less boilerplate. They may supervise parallel flows of machine work, edit generated artifacts, compose systems from agentic parts and step in mostly at moments of ambiguity or consequence. The chapter accepts all of that. It says none of it is the deeper role.
Five responsibilities
The deeper role is responsibility. The chapter lists what it covers:
Responsibility for standards.
Responsibility for scoping.
Responsibility for the boundaries within which machines act.
Responsibility for deciding when evidence is sufficient.
Responsibility for noticing when the system is producing motion without progress.

The last item shows why a machine cannot hold the role. A system that generates a lot of work looks busy. Someone must judge whether the work moved anything. A machine can report its own activity. It cannot answer for it.

This follows a theme from earlier in the chapter. Cheap generation shifts value upward, toward framing, discrimination, prioritization and the willingness to throw away seductive garbage. As output gets cheaper, standards do not become quaint. They become load-bearing. The people who hold those standards do the human work, even when they never touch a keyboard.
Why one name is a hard test
The six-month test is hard to dodge because it does not ask whether your team cares about quality. It asks for a single answer. A team or a role will not pass it. A name will.

The chapter draws a wider conclusion from this. It stays skeptical of both utopian and defensive stories. AI neither leaves engineering unchanged nor removes the need for engineers. It relocates value toward those who can design, govern and continuously improve systems of delegated work.
Run the test today

Pick one workflow where an agent produces output that others rely on. Imagine it is six months from now and the output is wrong. Write down the name of the person who answers for it. Use a person, not a team.
If you cannot write a name, treat that gap as engineering work, due before the next feature. If you can, write the name where the next reader of the system will see it.

title: A feature list agents cannot game
excerpt: A JSON file with three rules and an evidence field. How my Porto repo tracks features, and where the file stopped following its own rules.

children.text: An agent that is asked "are you done?" will often say yes. The answer costs nothing. So I do not ask. I keep a file that says what done means, and I check the file.
In the Porto repository, that file is
feature_list.json
The shape of an entry
Each feature has the same fields: an id, a priority, an area, a title, the user-visible behaviour, a status, a list of verification steps, a list of evidence, and a notes field.
Here is the first entry, trimmed. Its id is
porto-001

, its area is skeleton, and its title is "Engine fork, Porto config, shell, green build". Its user-visible behaviour is that the app runs for Porto and draws the terrain and city fabric. Its verification steps say to run the dev server, confirm that Porto is the default city and the terrain renders, and confirm that the build completes. Its evidence lists a commit, a passing
npm run verify
with the date, and a note that the config holds the core area and 70 landmark ids.
Notice the order. The behaviour comes first, in terms a user would see. Then the way to check it. Then the proof.
Three rules at the top
The file opens with three rules, each a boolean: only one feature is active at a time, passing requires evidence, and verification must not be skipped.

There are four statuses. Not started means work has not begun. In progress means the feature is the current task, or only part of it has shipped. Blocked means a documented blocker stops the work. Passing means the required verification passed and the evidence is recorded.

The rule that matters most is the second one. A status of passing without evidence is not allowed. This is what makes the list hard to game. To flip a feature to passing, an agent must write down a command, a file, or a count that someone else can check.
Where the file stopped following its rules
I read the file as I write this. It holds 31 features. 24 are passing and 7 are in progress.
The first rule says only one feature is active at a time. Seven are in progress.

The legend explains part of it. In progress also covers a feature where only part has shipped. But my clean-state checklist says exactly one feature should be in progress at the end of a session. The file and the checklist disagree.

There is a sharper mismatch. My session handoff from 5 October says two features, the quay walls and the building geometry detail levels, are not started. The feature list marks both as in progress. One of the two files is wrong, and nothing checks them against each other.

This is useful. The spec shows where the project drifted. Seven open items is a fact I can act on. The fix is either to split "partly shipped" into its own status, or to close the entries that are done. Both are small edits.
Why a file and not a chat
My
AGENTS.md

tells agents to prefer durable repository artifacts over chat summaries. A chat message disappears when the session ends. The feature list is in version control. A new session can read it, and a reviewer can read the history.
The same logic limits scope. If a task is not in the list, it is a new feature, and it gets an entry before it gets code.
Try it

Write three entries for a project you are working on. For each, write the behaviour a user would see, one check you could run, and what evidence would prove the check passed. If you struggle with the third part, the feature is not specified yet.

the definition of done is a command

title: A handoff note that fits on one screen
excerpt: The template I use to end every agent session, the checklist behind it, and the day my handoff grew to 2,681 words.

children.text: Agent sessions end. A usage limit hits, a context window fills, or I close the laptop. The next session starts with no memory of the last one. The handoff note is the only thing that crosses the gap.
The template
My Porto repository has a file called
session-handoff.md
. It says: compact note for the next session, keep it to one screen. It has eight fields.

The date. The session goal. The verified state, meaning the result of the last verify run. The active feature, by id. What changed. What is half-done or risky. The exact next step. And the files to look at first.
An example, from 5 October

On 5 October the note recorded that all 11 checks were green, with one transient smoke-test failure that passed on a rerun. The active feature was the deploy. The site was live at a temporary address, and the real domain did not answer yet.

Under "half-done or risky" it listed four things. Ten landmarks had no share image, though their pages referenced one. The engine sync script had never run. Two features had not started. And the smoke test needs a browser engine, or it skips.
Then the exact next step: run the share-image script, check that the folder holds 71 images, and add the domain in the hosting dashboard.
The last field is the sharpest. "Continue the work" tells the next session nothing. A command and a count tell it exactly what to do.
The checklist behind it

A second file, the clean-state checklist, lists eight things to do before ending a session. Verify passed, or the failure is recorded as the next task. The progress file is updated. The feature list is updated. No half-finished feature is loose, and work in progress is committed or stashed. Only intentional changes show in git status. Nothing ignored is staged. Exactly one feature is in progress. And the repository restarts from the init script.
The checklist exists so the handoff can be short. If the repository is in a clean state, the note does not need to explain a mess.
The day it did not fit
On 10 October I ran several agents in parallel on the same repository. When I stopped, I wrote a handoff for the day I would resume. It ran to 2,681 words.

It had to. It listed each agent, its port, its job, what it finished, and what it left half done. It named two deploy traps. It warned against shipping one branch. It recorded which verify checks failed. A one-screen note could not carry that.

I take two lessons from it. First, the one-screen rule works for one agent working on one feature. Parallel work breaks it, because the note must now describe several threads. Second, a long handoff is still better than none. But the length is a signal. It told me I had too much in flight.
A test
Open a fresh session with only your handoff note and the repository. Can the new session name the next step without asking you anything? If not, a field is missing.

specs shrink the search space

title: A minimum viable spec
excerpt: How small can a spec be and still work? Three fields from one entry of my feature list, a note on structure from the Kiro team, and a proposal.

children.text: My research notes on spec-driven development end with an open question: what is the minimum viable spec for a small task, compared with a large refactor? Here is my attempt to answer it, from files I use.
Nine fields, three that matter
An entry in my Porto feature list has nine fields: id, priority, area, title, user-visible behaviour, status, verification steps, evidence, and notes.

Six of them are bookkeeping. The id and the priority let an agent pick the next item. The area and the title let a person scan the list. The status says where the item stands. The notes field holds anything that does not fit elsewhere.
Three fields carry the spec itself. They are the behaviour a user would see, the steps that verify it, and the evidence that proves the steps passed.
My proposal
For a small task, write those three things and nothing more.
First, one sentence on what changes for the user, in terms the user would use. Second, one way to check it, a command or an exact step. Third, a place to record what the check printed.
If you cannot write the second one, the task is not ready for an agent. That is useful to learn in the first two minutes.

For a large refactor, the same three fields apply, but you split the work into many entries and add the constraints that must hold across all of them. The refactor's spec is a list of small specs, plus the rules that bind them.
I should say this is a proposal. I have not tested it against a range of project types, and I cannot say it is the right minimum for every team.
A note on structure
In
his Kiro talk

, Al Harris explains why the tool uses fixed templates for its three stages. The structure lets the team build reproducible tooling on top, such as task management in the interface. He also admits the structure is too rigid for some people. Some want to start from a technical note, such as a refactor where the requirements are not yet known, and extract the requirements later. The team was working on making the flow more flexible.
That tension is real. More structure gives tools something to hold. Less structure fits more kinds of work.
Keeping specs current

The second open question is how to keep specs current without process drag. My answer is to attach the update to something that already happens. My end-of-session checklist asks for the progress file and the feature list to be updated before the session ends. The update is part of finishing, not an extra chore.
My own files show the limit of that. Seven features are in progress against a rule of one. Habit helps, but it does not replace a check.
Who writes the spec

The third question is which parts a model writes. Harris shows one example: after working out a deployment detail the hard way, he asks the tool to write what it learned into a steering document, and says it usually does a good job. The model records. The person decides what is worth recording.
Try it today
Take one task from this week. Write the three fields. Ask an agent to do the task using only those three. See what it gets wrong. The gaps it finds are the next lines of your spec.
This is the last article in this series for now. It began with
what spec-driven development means to me

title: AGENTS.md is a map, not a manual
excerpt: The one file every agent reads first. What mine contains, why it points elsewhere instead of explaining everything, and where it broke its own rule.

children.text: Every one of my city map repositories has an
AGENTS.md
file at its root. In the Porto repository,
CLAUDE.md
is a three-line stub that says
AGENTS.md
is the single source of agent instructions. One file, so the tools cannot disagree.
The first line is a promise
The file states its own purpose: it is a map, not a manual. Read the pointer, then follow it. It asks to stay under about 100 lines, with detail kept in
README.md
PLAN.md
, or
docs/

The reason is attention. An agent reads this file at the start of every session. If it is long, the important rules compete with trivia. A short file with pointers gives the agent the shape of the project and tells it where each kind of detail lives.
What it contains
A startup workflow.

Six steps before any code is written: confirm the directory, read the progress file, read the feature list and pick the highest-priority unfinished feature, look at the last five commits, run the init script, and fix the baseline first if verification fails.
Working rules.

Work on one feature at a time. Do not mark a feature passing because code was added. Stay inside the feature's scope. Never hand-edit generated geodata, regenerate it through the pipeline. Do not silently weaken a check to make a feature pass. Prefer durable repository artifacts over chat summaries.
A definition of done.
A command,
npm run verify
, is the gate. The file lists the checks behind it and says what each one guards.
Hard constraints.
Node 22, plain ES modules, models authored in metres on real OSM footprints, free-licensed photos only.
An end-of-session routine.
Update the progress file and the feature list, record blockers, commit only in a safe state, and leave the repo ready to restart.
What is deliberately not in it
The file does not explain how the sea shader works, or why the terrain data looks the way it does. Those facts live in
perf/ARCHITECTURE.md
and in other documents. The map says where to look.
This matches advice I found in the research for my book. In
a talk on making codebases agent-ready
, Eno Reyes of Factory AI lists
AGENTS.md
files among the pillars of an agent-ready codebase, next to linters, tests, and reliable CI. The file matters, but it is one pillar of several.
Where it broke its own rule
I counted the lines. The Porto
AGENTS.md
has 137, and it asks to stay under about 100. The performance table and the command list grew it.

The content may earn its place. But the rule exists, and the file breaks it. This is a small example of spec drift: a spec that stops matching the thing it describes. The fix is either to move the table into
perf/
and link to it, or to change the rule. I have not done either yet.
A test for your own file
Give your
AGENTS.md

to someone who has never seen the project. Ask them to find three things in under a minute: how to run the checks, what counts as done, and what they must never edit by hand. If they cannot, the map has a hole.
Next:
a feature list agents cannot game

title: An evaluator rubric for AI changes
excerpt: Nine questions, scored 0 to 2, with three of them able to block a change on their own. The rubric I keep in my Porto repo.

children.text: A passing build tells you the code runs. It does not tell you the change is good. For that my repository holds a short rubric. Its first line says to use it after implementation and before final acceptance.
Nine categories
Each category is a question. The answer is a score from 0 to 2.

The first is the verify gate: did the full verify command run and end green, with the smoke test passing and not skipped? The second is the 1:1 fit: do the fit checks pass, and does every landmark still have its own hand-written builder? The third is the triangle budget.

The fourth is languages: do Russian, English, and Portuguese cover every new landmark, route, story chapter, and interface string? The fifth is data provenance: does every changed dimension entry carry sources with a fact and reasoning, and a confidence value? Was generated data rebuilt by the pipeline and not edited by hand?

The sixth is performance: does the change stay inside the load-time and frame-rate budget, and does the adaptive governor still step down on a slow device? The seventh is leftovers: does the change add no ids, coordinates, or text from Braga, the first city, outside inherited engine comments? The eighth is the web surface: do the sitemap, the landmark pages, and the share images stay in step with the landmark data, and do the API routes still answer? The ninth is scope and handoff: did the session stay inside the chosen feature, and do the state files hold true evidence?
What a score means

A 0 means the item is missing, failing, or has no evidence. A 1 means it is partly met, or met without recorded evidence. A 2 means it is fully met, with evidence in the repository: command output, a file path, or a count.
That last clause is the important one. A score of 2 needs proof that a reviewer can find. The rubric rewards written evidence as much as correct work.
The maximum is 18.
Three questions can block alone

The verdict has three levels. Accept needs 16 or more, with no zero in the verify gate, the 1:1 fit, or the triangle budget. Revise covers 10 to 15, or any zero outside those three. Block means below 10, or a zero in one of the three.
Those three guard the project's core promise: real scale and a working build. A change can be excellent everywhere else and still be unacceptable if it breaks them.
The rubric ends with three blanks to fill in: missing evidence, required fixes, and the next review trigger. A review that finds problems must say what to do next.
Why a rubric and not a feeling
A rubric moves the question from "does this sound finished?" to "can you show me?" It also makes reviews comparable. Two changes reviewed a month apart get the same nine questions.

My notes from the research for my book point the same way. Specs create eval seeds: the best evals often start as well-framed task definitions. This rubric is a small case of that. The questions came from the project's own rules.
What I have not measured

The rubric is a template in the repository. I have not recorded how often each category catches a problem, so I cannot tell you which question earns its place. If I tracked scores over several weeks, I would learn which rows to sharpen and which to drop.

a handoff note that fits on one screen

title: Five city maps in seven weeks: what the git log says about my pace
excerpt: Five real-scale 3D city maps, 453 commits, 48 days. The numbers, the bursts and pauses behind them, and why commit counts overstate what one person does.

children.text: How fast do I move? I counted.
The numbers

I build real-scale 3D maps of Portuguese cities. Five repositories share one engine. The first commit was on 28 September, in the Braga repository. The most recent was on 14 November. That is 48 days, about seven weeks.
Across the five repositories there are 453 commits. By repository, Braga has 60, Guimarães 40, Barcelos 51, Porto 112, and the fifth city 190.

By 10 October, four of them were live with 134 places in total: Braga 30, Guimarães 18, Barcelos 16, and Porto 70. Porto is the flagship, with real streets, a coastline from OpenStreetMap, and models of all its landmarks. A fifth city followed in late October.
Bursts and pauses

Commits did not arrive evenly. Counting by calendar week, the weeks of 28 September and 5 October brought 98 and 139 commits. The next two weeks brought 5 and 1. Then 136, 66, and 8 in the last, partial week.
Only 26 of the 48 days have any commit at all. The busiest day, 30 October, has 95 commits.

The gap in the middle is real. Work paused for about two weeks after the second week and resumed in late October. My notes record that agent rounds can die when usage limits hit, and that my 10 October stop was written as a handoff for that reason. They do not say why the gap lasted two weeks. The pace is not a smooth line. It is a series of sprints and stops.
What a commit count hides
I want to be careful here. Commits are a poor measure of progress.

First, agents wrote most of the code. I direct the work, define the checks, and decide what ships. My agents type. A commit count measures the output of a team of agents, and I am the lead of that team. It says little about how much one person writes.
Second, commits vary in size. A commit that fixes one typo counts the same as one that adds a coastline. And agents commit often, so a busy day can inflate the count.

Third, the numbers do not measure quality. The same repositories contain a failed soak test, a branch that nearly shipped by mistake, and features that are only half done. I have written about those too.
What I would call speed
If I have to choose one number, I would not pick commits. I would pick this: five working maps, each with its own live site and its own checks, in seven weeks, by one person directing agents.

What made it possible was not typing speed. It was the structure around the agents: a shared engine, a repository per city, a verify command, a feature list, and handoff notes that let a stopped session resume. I describe those files in my series on spec-driven development, which starts with
what spec-driven development means to me
Where it is slow

Some things do not speed up. Real-device testing is still on my list. Language editions made by machine translation need a native reader. A few decisions, such as licences for generated art, are mine alone, and they wait for me.
Pace is a property of the whole system. The agents are fast. The checks, the decisions, and the review set the speed of the loop.

title: Mentoring the machine: outcomes, context, constraints, evaluation
excerpt: Eric Hou of Augment Code calls AI a perpetually junior engineer. What that role asks of you, and how it maps to the files in a spec-driven repo.

children.text: A spec is what you hand to a colleague who is capable but new. That image comes from
a talk by Eric Hou
, a member of technical staff at Augment Code.
The perpetual junior

Hou describes AI as a perpetually junior engineer. It has no knowledge of your organisation or your systems. It can implement something in isolation. It needs a structured environment to do well. Unlike a human junior, it works through a task in minutes, but it forgets between conversations.

From this he draws a role for the engineer: the perpetual tech lead. Stop assigning tickets. Start mentoring. A mentor gives outcomes, context, constraints, and evaluation, and does not dictate the implementation.
Those four words are close to a definition of a spec.
His story, as he tells it

Hou anchors the talk in a Tuesday where three things collide: an overdue design-system component, a staging emergency caused by a library mismatch, and a new colleague asking for help. He describes handing the component to an agent early, running log parsing and a search for the bad commit in parallel across two agents, and pointing the new colleague to a chat assistant that can read the code, the documents, and the tickets.

His headline result is a library upgrade across 12 services and 20,000 lines of code. By his account it was finished, tested, and ready for final human polish in roughly half a day, against a normal estimate of three weeks. These are his numbers about his work. I cannot check them.
Why teams stall

He makes a sharp point about scale. Individuals gain a lot, but teams stall. The reason is the same context deficit that makes a new hire take months to become useful. He reports that four in five engineers name missing context as their biggest blocker, and that this predates AI. You cannot give an agent the knowledge your team never wrote down.

His three starting steps are to gather knowledge by auditing the documents you have, to get familiar by introducing tools across teams, and to lean in by sharing what works, including agent memories and task lists.
Mapping it to files
Here is how his four words map onto the files in my Porto repository.
Outcomes live in the user-visible behaviour of each entry in the feature list. Context lives in
AGENTS.md

, which says where to start, and in the plan and the architecture notes. Constraints live in the hard-constraints section and in the checks, such as the rule that a model never shrinks below 97 percent of its real size. Evaluation lives in the verify command and in the evaluator rubric.
I am not claiming Hou uses these files. The mapping is mine. But it shows that a spec-driven repository is mentoring written down, so the next session, which has no memory, can still be mentored.
A small exercise

Think of a task you would give a new colleague on their first day. Write the four things you would tell them: the outcome, what they need to know, what they must not do, and how you will judge the result. That page is a spec.

when the spec is not enough

title: My rules for working with coding agents
excerpt: The rules in my own agent configuration, with the reason wherever my notes give one.

children.text: I keep a global instructions file that every one of my agent sessions reads. A section of it is headed with the date of an opportunity scan on 28 September. Here are the rules in it. Where my notes give a reason, I give it too.
Run sessions in short loops

One session per pull request. Start a fresh session after a merge, and do not resume a session older than a day. The review found five sessions that had run for weeks, at over one million tokens per turn. A long session is expensive, and its context fills with old details.
Edit files with the right tool
File changes go through the edit and write tools, not through shell heredocs. The shell runs things. It does not write source files.
Never sleep in a command
Do not use
sleep

inside a shell call. Wait with a purpose-built tool, a monitor with an until-loop, or a background run. A guard on my shell blocks sleep chains. Its message says polling with sleep burned 47 blocked calls and 27 loops in past sessions.
Treat a denial as a decision
When the permission classifier blocks a command, do not issue it again. Give the exact command to the person to run themselves, and carry on with other work. A block is a decision, not an obstacle.
Answer once, in the right language
Reply once, in the language of the last message. Do not repeat the answer in a second language.
Stop on re-authorisation
When a tool server says it needs re-authorisation, stop and ask for the settings command. Do not retry.
Look at what you made
View every generated image or asset before reporting it done.
Read big files in windows
Never read a large file whole. Search for the symbol, then read a window. A guard blocks whole-file reads above 1,200 lines.
Keep secrets out of reports

When a subagent finds a credential anywhere, it reports the fact and the location, never the value. A secret quoted in a subagent's report lands in the parent transcript, and no hook can remove it afterwards.
Commit messages carry no AI attribution
My commit messages do not include co-author or attribution lines for the AI. That is a style choice about authorship on my own repositories.
The orchestrator role

The same file describes how I run delegation. I act as the orchestrator: plan, decompose, delegate, and synthesise, and keep my own context lean. Reasoning-heavy work goes to a deep-reasoning agent. Mechanical work goes to a fast worker. For a fresh angle, I may ask a second engineering agent from another vendor. For high-stakes decisions, I may give the same problem to two agents without showing either the other's answer, then combine the best of both.
Why write these down

A new session has no memory of the last one. The file is what it reads first. That is the same idea as the rest of this blog: a spec for the agent, written once, read every time. If you are new to it, start with
what spec-driven development means to me

title: Quality means fewer defects
excerpt: Josh Albrecht of Imbue defines code quality by defects and time to fix. His prevention and detection techniques, and where my own repos show the same drift he targets.

children.text: "High quality code" is a phrase that means nothing until you define it. In
a talk on writing high-quality code with AI
, Josh Albrecht, the CTO of Imbue, does define it. He borrows from software engineering research: quality is the absence of defects, measured by how many there are and how long they take to fix.
Feedback before the pull request

Albrecht presents Sculptor, a research-preview environment for coding agents that Imbue built. A key choice is when feedback arrives. A pull request review is too late, he argues. Sculptor gives synchronous, immediate feedback while the agent works.
Four ways to prevent defects
He describes four prevention strategies.

The agent researches prior art before it writes code. A plan-only step comes first, enforced through the system prompt, so no code appears before there is a plan. Specs and documents are first-class artifacts, and the tool detects drift between a document and the code. And a strict style guide applies, in a functional and immutable style, including one tailored to common mistakes of AI agents.
Three ways to detect them
On the detection side he covers linters, tests, and review by a model.
For linters, the tool compares the issues that existed before with the issues the change introduced. The agent is not blamed for old lint debt.

For tests, he argues the old objections to writing them have faded. An agent can generate hundreds or thousands of synthetic inputs for the unhappy paths and flag outputs that look wrong. Generated unit tests that go stale are often worth throwing away and regenerating. And integration tests written from user-facing test plans are usually more valuable than unit tests.
For review, you can ask a model to check for style or spec violations, or for missing details, before the commit.
He closes with a tactic: run many sandboxed attempts at a fix in parallel and keep the one that succeeds. His logic is that a problem well stated is half solved.
Where I recognise this
The idea of doc-code drift is one I have lived with. My
AGENTS.md

asks to stay under about 100 lines and has 137. My feature list says one feature is active at a time and marks seven in progress. My handoff from 5 October calls two features not started, while the list marks them in progress. Each is a spec and its subject drifting apart. A check that compares them would find all three in seconds.

The lint idea carries over to my gate. A check that fails on old problems teaches an agent to ignore failures. A check that reports only what the change introduced keeps the signal clean. My verify script reports PASS, FAIL, or SKIP for each check. It has no step that separates old failures from new ones. That is a gap.
A practical start
Pick one drift your project already has. Write a ten-line script that detects it. Run the script in your verify step. Then a check, not a reader, notices when the spec and the code drift apart.

mentoring the machine

title: Requirements a machine can check
excerpt: Structured requirements, EARS syntax, and property-based testing turn a sentence into an invariant. Notes from a Kiro talk, and one rule from my own map project.

children.text: A requirement written as a paragraph can be read in three ways. A requirement written as a rule can be checked. This article is about moving from the first to the second.
What the Kiro team does
In
his talk on spec-driven development

, Al Harris explains that the Kiro IDE turns a prompt into requirements with acceptance criteria. It writes those criteria in the EARS format. EARS stands for the Easy Approach to Requirements Syntax. It is a structured form of natural language, so each requirement has a clear trigger and a clear response.

He says this looked like an interesting but minor choice for the first months. Then the team started using it. The requirements translate into properties of the system. A property is an invariant, something that must always hold.
Properties and property-based testing

Property-based testing checks an invariant by searching for a counterexample. The test generates many inputs and looks for one that breaks the rule. Libraries such as Hypothesis for Python and fast-check for Node do this. If the search finds nothing, you gain confidence that the rule holds.

Harris is careful about the word "confidence". It depends on how well the tests are written. A weak generator proves little. Still, the chain is useful: a requirement becomes a property, and the property becomes a test that runs on every change. The requirement stays connected to the code.
He also describes a step before testing: scanning the requirements themselves for ambiguity and for constraints that conflict, and helping the author resolve them.
A rule from my own project
My city maps are built at real scale. One rule says a landmark model must never shrink below its real size. In prose, it reads as a wish. In the repository it is a check called
check:fit

, with two hard-fail rules. A model fails if it deviates from its OpenStreetMap footprint by more than 15 percent. It also fails if it covers less than 97 percent of the OSM extent, or of the real height recorded in
dimensions.json

Written in the EARS style, the second rule reads: while a landmark model is built, the system shall keep it at 97 percent or more of the OSM extent and of the recorded height. The EARS wording is mine, not a format my repository uses. But the shape fits. There is a state, a subject, and a response you can measure.
Because it is a check, the rule does not depend on anyone's memory. An agent that draws a landmark too small gets a failed build.
Not every requirement checks this way

Many entries in my feature list still end in a manual step, such as "open the local server and confirm that the terrain renders". A person or a browser script has to look. Some qualities, such as whether a view feels right, resist a property.
Push each requirement as far toward a check as it will go. When it will not go further, write the manual step down plainly.
A short method

Take one requirement from a current project. Rewrite it with a condition, a subject, and a measurable response. Ask what single counterexample would prove it false. If you can name one, you can write the check. If you cannot, the requirement is still ambiguous. Find that out before an agent builds on it.
The next article,
AGENTS.md as a map
, covers the file that tells an agent where these checks live.

title: Specs shrink the search space
excerpt: Why explicit boundaries help parallel agents, how I split work by file ownership, and what happened when two agents shared a file.

children.text: The first pattern in my notes on spec-driven development reads: good specs shrink the search space. An agent that knows the goal, the boundary, and the check has fewer wrong moves to try.
Boundaries as specs

On my city map projects, I split parallel agents by file ownership. One group owns the landmark models, the fit checks, and the landmark list. One owns the scene, the effects, and the interface. One owns the data folder. An agent edits only its own files.
That is a spec. It says what an agent may touch. It turns "build the sea shader" from an open problem into one with edges.

On 10 October I had five agents working in the same Porto working tree at once, each with a job and a port for its dev server. The handoff I wrote that day listed the rules for all of them: write to disjoint files, commit only your own files, do not push, do not deploy.
Structure helps the agent read the code too
In
his Kiro talk

, Al Harris answers a question about large existing codebases. His answer is that it depends, but one factor stands out. If the system already separates concerns well, and its components are highly cohesive, the agent can say "this module does this thing" and need not hold 18 things in context. A codebase with a lot of tech debt makes it harder for the agent to find its way, as it does for a person. He adds that reliable tests and clear module separation both make the agent perform better.

He also describes how a task list runs. By default each task starts as a fresh session that shares no context with the earlier ones. The session is seeded with the specification, then told to do one task. The spec is the memory.
Where the boundary leaked

A boundary only works if it holds. In my 10 October handoff, two files were shared. Two agents had both left unfinished edits in the scene file and in the landmarks file. The handoff warns that whoever commits those files includes both authors' changes, so they must be committed together, after the verify run.

Another leak was smaller. The terrain agent owned the fit file. The landmark agent found a dead fit rule for the Felgueiras landmark in it and restored the file byte for byte, since the file was not its own. Yet the terrain agent had edited a rule for the Palácio de Cristal in the same file, and that landmark was the landmark agent's area. The handoff records these as deviations to reconcile.

This shows that a file-ownership rule needs a way to handle changes that cross it. The rule said who owns a file. It did not say what to do when a change belongs to one agent and sits in another's file.
A cheap test

For each parallel task, write one sentence about which files it may edit. If two sentences name the same file, decide who owns it before you start. On 10 October, two shared files had to be committed together after the verify run.
Next:
quality means fewer defects

title: The definition of done is a command
excerpt: One command gates every change in my map projects. What it runs, why it skips missing inputs instead of faking them, and why Eno Reyes calls coverage a hard limit for agents.

children.text: In my Porto repository, a feature is done when
npm run verify
passes. Not when the code looks right, not when an agent says so. The command builds the app and runs every check whose input data exists.
What the gate runs

The gate runs 11 checks. They cover the build and the content contract for landmarks, routes, licences, and photos. They check the geometry: footprints, buildings, terrain. They check real-world dimensions and their sources. They check the 1:1 fit against OpenStreetMap. They check the street network and traffic. They check the triangle budget for every model, from 4,000 to 40,000 triangles each and 900,000 in total. Then a smoke test loads the built site in a headless browser and fails on console errors, graphics errors, or bad geometry buffers. Smaller smoke tests cover the trams and the rail.
A feature counts as done under four conditions, all written in
AGENTS.md

. The user-visible behaviour is implemented. The verify command was actually run and passed. Evidence is recorded in the feature list and the progress file. And the repository restarts cleanly from the init script.
Skipped, not faked
One line in the file stands out: missing inputs are skipped, not faked.

If the data a check needs does not exist, the check skips. It does not invent a pass. The smoke test shows the cost. It needs a browser engine installed, and without one it reports SKIP. My evaluator rubric then refuses to count a SKIP as a pass. The rubric asks whether the smoke test passed and was not skipped.
A gate that quietly passes when it cannot run is worse than no gate. It gives a false green, and agents learn to trust it.
The temptation to weaken the check

There is a second rule beside it: do not silently weaken the verification script, or a single check, to make a feature pass. The easy path for an agent that fails a check is to adjust the check. The rule makes that a visible act, not a quiet one.
Why this gets harder for teams
In
a talk on making codebases agent-ready

, Eno Reyes argues that agents fail in many real projects not because the models are weak, but because the codebase lacks the automatic validation agents need. His starting point is that software has an unusually good signal for correctness: tests, linters, and continuous integration.

His sharpest observation concerns tolerance. Many organisations function with 50 to 60 percent test coverage, because people compensate by hand. A flaky build that fails every third run is a nuisance a human works around. For an agent, it is a hard block. The agent cannot tell a real failure from noise.
He proposes eight areas to audit: linter quality,
AGENTS.md

files, test coverage, flaky-test rate, API and doc completeness, reliability of the CI signal, automated code review, and dependency hygiene. He also argues that an imperfect AI-written test is better than none, because it records a specification that later agents can follow and improve. And he claims that organisations that invest in this validation see gains of five to seven times, not one and a half or two. That figure is his claim. I report it, I do not endorse it.
My own gaps
Reading his list against my repository, I can confirm two items: there is an
AGENTS.md
, and there is a gate with 11 checks. I cannot confirm the others from the files I have in front of me. For example, I do not have a measured flaky-test rate. That is a fair place to begin an audit.
Next:
an evaluator rubric for AI changes

title: What spec-driven development means to me
excerpt: A working definition of spec-driven development, how it differs from paperwork, and the files I use to practise it in my own projects. Part 1 of a series.

children.text: This is the first article in a series about spec-driven development, or SDD. I will keep it practical. Each article takes one idea and shows where it lives in my own repositories.
A working definition

In my book research I wrote down this definition. Spec-driven development makes task intent, constraints, acceptance criteria, and system boundaries explicit enough that humans and agents can implement against them reliably.

Two words in that sentence matter. The first is "explicit". A spec states what you would otherwise leave in your head. The second is "against". A spec is something you build against and check against. If nobody ever compares the result with the spec, it is only a document.
Why vague requests got more dangerous

When coding agents were weak, a vague request produced a weak result, and you noticed at once. Now agents are strong. A vague request produces a confident, plausible result that may solve a different problem. The cost of a missing constraint went up, because the agent will carry on without it.

My notes put it this way: specs convert ambiguous desire into executable coordination. They help people agree with each other. They help agents avoid sprawl. They help evals decide whether a change is correct.
Not bureaucracy, and not a PRD
Two distinctions from my notes guard against the wrong reading.
First, SDD is not about producing more documents. The goal is a clearer execution contract. If a document does not change what an agent does or how a reviewer judges, delete it.
Second, an ordinary product requirements document is usually not enough. Many are too narrative, too vague, or too incomplete to guide an agent.
One public example
Al Harris, a principal engineer at Amazon, described the approach his team built into the Kiro IDE in
a conference talk

. The flow takes a prompt and turns it into three artifacts: requirements with acceptance criteria, a design, and a task list. He describes the spec as the artifacts that represent the state of the system at a point in time, plus a structured workflow, plus tools on top that make results reproducible.
He treats the spec as something that moves through three stages, not as a single file written once.
What it looks like in my repos
My city map projects carry their spec in plain files at the root of each repository.
AGENTS.md
tells an agent where to start and what the rules are.
PLAN.md
holds the plan and the remaining rounds.
feature_list.json
lists the features with how to verify each one.
evaluator-rubric.md
scores a finished change.
session-handoff.md
and a clean-state checklist carry the work from one session to the next.
None of these is long. Each answers one question for an agent that has never seen the project: where do I start, what is next, how do I prove it works, how do I judge it, and what do I leave behind.
The series
The next articles take these files one at a time, and then look at what other practitioners say about the same problems.
I start with
requirements a machine can check
, then
AGENTS.md as a map
and
a feature list agents cannot game
. Later articles cover the definition of done, the rubric, the handoff, and the limits of all of this.
The thread through the series is simple. Cheap generation does not remove the need for judgement. It moves the judgement into the spec.

title: When the spec is not enough
excerpt: A green gate, a branch that passed 15 of 15 checks and would have rolled back live work, and an invented number that no check covers. The limits of spec-driven development in my own repos.

children.text: A series about spec-driven development should say where it fails. Here is where it failed for me.
A green gate that was not complete

On 10 October an agent produced a branch with lazy-loaded models and a lite scene. It passed all 15 of its verify checks. It was not safe to ship. The branch left out the camera clamp, the boat models, the finer terrain, the landing pads, and the first wave of commits. Deploying it would have rolled back live work.
The gate answered "does this branch work?" It had no way to answer "does this branch contain everything that is already live?" Nobody had written that requirement down, so nothing checked it.
A spec that does not cover deploying

Two more traps lived outside the checks. One commit imported a file that only arrived in the next commit, so deploying the state between them would have broken the build. And the real build command edits one of the tracked data files before it builds. Both were in my handoff, in prose. Neither was a check.
A spec covers what you thought to specify. Deploying is a separate job, and my specs did not cover it.
The main branch failing its own gate

The same handoff records that the main branch failed two verify checks at that point. One was a life-simulation smoke test, broken by a boat hull change. The other was the model check, because one of the 70 models fell outside the triangle range. The gate did its job. It caught regressions from a busy day. But it also shows that a gate can be red while work continues around it.
An invented number no check covers

My notes record that the storey count for buildings without a tag is an invented heuristic. OpenStreetMap does not say how many storeys such buildings have, so the code guesses. I decided to ship it. No check can tell me whether the guess is right, because there is nothing to compare it against. The spec records the guess, and that is all a spec can do here.
Small drifts

I described three drifts earlier in the series. The agent instructions file is longer than the limit it states. The feature list has seven features in progress, against its own one-at-a-time rule. A handoff and the list disagree on whether two features have started.
The open questions

My research notes end with questions I cannot yet answer. What is the minimum viable spec for a small task, compared with a large refactor? How can a team keep specs current without creating process drag? Which parts of a spec should a model write, and which a human?
I have partial answers, and the next article gives one.
What I take from it
A spec is a set of promises. Checks keep the promises you can measure. For the rest, such as completeness, deploy order, and judgement calls, you need a written warning and a person who reads it.

a minimum viable spec

title: A 200 is not enough to call a city live
excerpt: Two of my map addresses answered with other people's sites. How that changed the rule for what "live" means, and why my maps now live on subdomains.

children.text: On 14 November I tested the addresses I had planned for two new maps.
lisboa-3d.vercel.app
and
faro-3d.vercel.app
both answered with a normal 200. Both were other people's sites.
Names on
*.vercel.app
are first come, first served. A plain "does it answer?" check would have called both of my cities live. A visitor would have landed on a stranger's page.
The rule
The README now states it: a place counts as live when its address answers 200 with one of our city maps that names it. A 200 alone is not enough.
Two commands enforce the rule.
npm run check
validates the city data and the landmarks, and every place marked live must answer.
npm run check:live
tests every address and prints which
live
flags are wrong.
How a map names itself

Each place record has a ready flag, or null when the site exposes none. Some maps run on a different engine and have no such flag. Madeira and Pena Park are two. For those, the record lists the marks that appear in the page
<title>
, and the check looks for them.
The check does not judge quality. It answers one question: is this page ours, and does it name this place?
"Coming soon" never links
A place that is not live shows a card with a clear label. The card is an
<article>
that can take focus but has no link. A visitor cannot click through to a dead or foreign page. The check and the card enforce the same promise from two sides.
The fix: subdomains of my own domain
On 15 November I told the agent to decide everything itself. It chose a subdomain for each new map:
https://<name>.portugal-3d.com
, with
douro
for Pinhão. Subdomains of my own domain cannot belong to a stranger.
The setup needs one wildcard DNS record at the registrar. I added it. After that, each repository gets its own deploy, and the subdomain is attached to it with
vercel domains add
. Then I run the live check and flip the
live
flag.

Until the wildcard existed, the globe linked the eleven new maps at their Vercel addresses. Two of those names carried a suffix that Vercel had added, because the plain names were taken. When the record went live, all eleven subdomains served their maps with certificates. The globe switched its links to the subdomains.
On 16 November I moved Guimarães, Barcelos and Arouca to subdomains too. Braga and Porto keep their own domains,
braga-3d.com
and
porto-3d.com
. Pena Park stays on its Vercel address.
What I take from it
Test the claim, not the status code. "Does it return 200?" and "is this our page?" are different questions. Only the second one protects a visitor.
Own the namespace. A shared hostname is fine for a prototype. For a public front door, put every address under a name you control.
Keep the check in the repository, so the command knows which flags are right.
The next article covers
what happens after a visitor picks a city

title: A globe in front of eighteen maps
excerpt: How portugal-3d.com went from an idea on 5 November to the front door of eighteen real-scale 3D maps. What it is, how it is built, and what the git log says about the pace.

children.text: By early November I had five city maps and no front door. Each map lived at its own address. A visitor had to know the address first.

On 5 November I described a different shape to my agent. A globe, or a sphere, with the 3D cities on it. Pick any city. It should be a standalone project on its own domain, portugal-3d.com. Scroll a little and the globe moves with you, then a city gets selected.
This article is the first in a series about that site. It covers what the site is and how fast it came together.
What it is

The README describes it in one paragraph. It is the front door to eighteen real-scale 3D maps of Portugal, from Ponte de Lima to Faro and out to Madeira. A scroll-driven globe pulls the visitor toward Portugal and highlights the outline. Every place shows as a pin. A focused place shows its best-known landmarks, its UNESCO listing, and the straight-line distance to its neighbours. A pick plays a dive that ends in that place's own site.
A place whose site is not up shows as "coming soon". It never sends anyone to a dead page.
One list of places
data/cities.json

is the only list of places. It runs north to south by region. A record holds an id, a region, and a rank that sets label priority. It holds the names and a short fact in six languages, and the fact's source: a URL and a quoted passage. It holds the coordinates, the map's address, a
live
flag, a card image, a theme colour, and the UNESCO listing if there is one.
The README says plainly that four of the six languages are machine translations. Spanish, French, German and Russian need a native review. I have not done that review yet.
HTML first, globe second
The cards for all places are written into
index.html
at build time, grouped by region in one sideways rail. They work with script off, with reduced motion, and on a device without WebGL. Script then adds the globe on top.
A small module picks one of three tiers for the globe: full, lite or static. Phones always get lite. The next article in the series, on
the draw-call budget
, shows what that costs.
The pace, from git
The repository has 62 commits. They fall on six days.

On 7 November: 13 commits. The design and plan came first, then the scaffold, the static landing, and the globe scene. Then a gap with no commits until 13 November. That is the day I bought the domain. On the 13th: 13 commits. On the 14th: 15 commits, with sixteen pins, collision-aware labels, and a panel with landmarks and distances. On the 15th: 6 commits, and all sixteen maps went live. On the 16th: 6 commits. On the 17th: 9 commits.
The count grew from five places to eighteen. Madeira joined as the seventeenth place on 15 November. Pena Park joined as the eighteenth on 17 November.
I do not read commit counts as effort. An agent writes most of the code. What they show is rhythm: a burst, a pause, then three days of steady work.
What came out of it
The rest of the series takes one piece at a time:
A 200 is not enough to call a city live
Scroll, dive, and the way back
Labels that do not collide
Claims with a status
Eleven city maps in three days, and the limits behind them
What my Claude sessions show about my own work
The lesson from the first week is small. Start the front door with a list in plain HTML. The globe is a layer on top of the list, not a replacement for it.

title: Claims with a status
excerpt: Every statement on my globe story has a status (works, trying, idea) and a source file. How the check works, and what a claims list found when I turned it on my own pages.

children.text: A tourism site that says "tested on phones" when it was not tells a small lie. My globe keeps its sentences in a file that makes this kind of sentence hard to write.
The story is data
The globe tells a story in six chapters as you scroll. The text does not live in the page. It lives in two files.
data/claims.json
holds each statement as a record with a status and a source. The status is one of three words:
works
trying
, or
idea
data/story.json
builds the chapters out of claim ids.
Today the file holds nine claims. Six are
works
, one is
trying
, and two are
idea
One rule for adding a sentence
To add a statement, add a claim with a source. If there is no source, mark it
idea
and word it as an idea. Only then list its id in a chapter. The wording of an
idea
must read like one.
A check that opens the sources
The command
npm run check:story
validates the data. It checks that every source file exists. The paths are relative to my development folder. It then writes
docs/story-claims.md
, a plain list for me to review.
The check cannot tell me that a source supports the sentence. It can only tell me that a source exists. The written list exists so that I read it.
The same habit on another page

I used the same method on a page for institutions that I have not linked from the site yet. For each line in its "works today" column, I wrote down which file proves it. I checked by reading the code of each map. For that column I did not open the live sites, and the list says so.
The list also has a "left out" section.
A guide that answers questions is built but parked. It loads only with
?guide=1
, and no API key is set, so it has never answered a real question.
"Tested on phones" stays out. No map has had a test on a real phone.
A statement that a trail is official stays out. Its official status is not confirmed.
"Reconstructions are labelled" stays out. No map shows a reconstruction label yet.
What a claims list finds

Two sentences changed on 17 November when Pena Park joined. "Day and night on every map" became "on the town maps and Madeira", because Pena Park has no night. "Weather on every map except Madeira" became "on the town maps", because Madeira and Pena Park have none.
The list also counted photos. Eight of the 301 town-map landmarks have no photo. So "a photo for every landmark" is false, and the page says "a photo where a free one exists".
The list records conflicts between sources. One map's README still says "not deployed", while its progress log and data say the map is built. The page follows the progress log and the data.
