eleven city maps in three days, and the limits behind them

title: Eleven city maps in three days, and the limits behind them
excerpt: Sintra, Faro, Lisboa, Évora, Coimbra and six more went from nothing to live between 13 and 15 November. What made it fast, and the four limits that decided the pace.

children.text: The globe needed more places on it. Between 13 and 15 November, eleven new city maps went from nothing to live. This article explains how, and what held the pace down.
The waves
Each map is a fork of the same engine. I built them in three waves, with agents.

On 13 November: Sintra, Faro, Lisboa, and Ponte de Lima. On 14 November, a UNESCO wave: Évora, Coimbra, Tomar, and Belém. Later that day, a third wave: Batalha, Alcobaça, and Pinhão, where the Douro vineyard terraces are drawn in the ground shader.
All eleven passed
npm run verify
on 14 November. On 15 November, all sixteen maps were deployed and linked from the globe. Madeira followed as the seventeenth the same day.
Limit one: usage
The agents run on a plan with a five-hour usage limit. Four heavy agents in parallel use it up. Three or four at once hit it again on 15 November. Two at once was safe.

Two rules now go into my briefs. Commit after each round, so a cut-off loses little. And for a repository that I might deploy, work in a git worktree and leave the merge to me. After the merge, remove the worktree, so the deploy tool does not upload it.
Limit two: the map data

The pipeline asks a public service, Overpass, for the OpenStreetMap data. Overpass was down at times. A script in two of the repositories can answer the same queries from the main OpenStreetMap API when you set
OSM_API=1
The result is uneven. On some maps the outer ring of OpenStreetMap data is thin because Overpass failed. Each repository records the commands to resume. Most building heights are estimates.
Limit three: what a site lets you read
Some heritage and tourism sites refuse automated reads. I did not work around that. The agents do not pretend to be a browser to get past a refusal.

The photo script for Belém rejects Commons authors who ask to be contacted before reuse. The globe uses 33 landmark photos from the city repositories, each with a checked licence and a visible credit. Eight of 301 town-map landmarks still have no photo.
Limit four: measurement
When the eleven maps first passed
verify

, I had not run the performance bench on them. That is a gap. On 15 November, the faster-start work from Lisboa was ported into the other ten. In the test profile "phone-low", the first frame arrived at about 5.5 seconds, down from about 8. That figure comes from a test profile, not a real phone.
What made it fast

The engine was shared. A map is mostly data: a city config, landmark records, and a data pipeline that is resumable and writes into the repository. The checks from the first city came along, and all eleven forks passed them on 14 November.
The last article in this series looks at the logs behind all of this:
what my Claude sessions show about my own work

title: Labels that do not collide
excerpt: Eighteen pins on a small country. The rules that merge, place and hide labels, and the tests that run them at four screen sizes in two languages.

children.text: Portugal is a narrow country. At the full view of the globe, several of my eighteen places sit almost on top of each other. Naive labels would pile up into an unreadable smear. This article covers the rules that stop that.
Merge close places
Every frame,
src/labels.js
looks at the pins on screen. Places that sit closer than 30 pixels merge under the name of the best-ranked one. The label reads like "Lisbon +2".
Rank is a field in the data. Rank 1 wins. The focused place always leads its group, whatever its rank.
Place what is left

Each label tries eight sides around its pin. It takes the first side that is clear of other labels, other pins, the info panel, the chapter text, and the bar. If no side is clear, the label hides. The pin's button keeps its name.
Zoom a group
A click on a merged group zooms the camera until the places in it stand apart. "Back to all of Portugal" or the Escape key returns to the full view.
Featured places follow the same rules

One place, Pena Park, carries a "Featured" badge and a gold ring on its pin. A featured place follows its rank like any other. At the country view, Pena Park has rank 18 and sits inside the group "Pinhão +1". Its gold ring shows when you hover over it, focus it, zoom to it, or when its card is in view in the rail.
The panel and the arcs

The place panel shows the focused place's landmarks, its UNESCO mark, and its three nearest places with great-circle distances. It also draws fine arcs to those neighbours in an SVG laid over the canvas. The arcs cost no extra draw calls.
On a phone, the card in view in the rail focuses its place. The visitor scrolls cards, and the globe follows.
Tests
Layout rules are easy to break without noticing. The repository covers them from three sides.

A unit test file checks the merge and placement logic. An end-to-end test checks label overlap at four screen sizes, in English and in Russian. Other end-to-end tests cover the panel, the distances and the arcs, and the card-in-view focus on a phone. The Russian copy ran long, so it was shortened to fit a small phone.
Lesson
Write layout rules as code, then test them in the longest language at the smallest size.
The next article is about the words on the page:
claims with a status

title: Scroll, dive, and the way back
excerpt: How scroll drives the globe, how a pick becomes a dive into a separate site, and the three values that let a city link back without confusing a visitor who never saw the globe.

children.text: The globe page has to do three jobs. It has to follow the scroll. It has to hand a visitor to a city's own site without a seam. And it has to let that visitor come back.
Scroll as the only input
One module,
src/timeline.js
, maps scroll progress to everything on screen: the camera, the glow on Portugal's outline, the dimming, the opener, the six story chapters, and the fade-in of the cards.
The hero spacer is 600vh tall. Progress runs from 0 to 1 over that height. The opener takes up to 0.12. The six chapters run from 0.12 to 0.84. The cards take the last part, 0.84 to 1.
A function of one number is easy to test. The repository has a unit test file for the timeline and an end-to-end scroll test. The end-to-end test does what a visitor does: it scrolls.
The opener
A short hero video plays at the start.
src/opener.js
loads it after the globe is ready, plays it once, and stops it when it has faded. A helper called
pickOpener
decides whether the video plays at all. It plays only on the full tier and only if the visitor has not asked to save data. Otherwise only the poster shows.
The dive
When a visitor picks a place,
src/dive.js
plays a descent. The shot ends at the city's own address with two values added:
?intro=1&lang=<lang>&from=globe
. The city site plays its own fly-in as the last part of the shot. The two animations meet in the middle, so the visitor sees one movement.
The dive needs very little from the other site: an address and a theme colour. That is why it works for Madeira and Pena Park, which run on a different engine.
The way back
A visitor who clicked through from the globe should be able to return. A visitor who found a city through a search engine should not see a link to a globe they never saw.
The
from=globe
value solves this. Each city repository carries
src/back-to-globe.js
. It shows the back link only when the address contains
from=globe
. The link points to
https://portugal-3d.com/#from=<id>
, and
src/ascend.js
on the globe reads that value and flies back to the right place.
So three values carry the whole contract:
intro
lang
, and
from
Where the contract has a hole
Pena Park has no ready flag and no back link to the globe. The README states both facts. The dive still works for it, because the dive needs only an address and a theme.
Tests
The repository has a unit test for the dive and one for the return path. An end-to-end test covers the return. Together they cover the loop: pick, dive, arrive, return.
The next article looks at what all of this costs on a phone:
the globe costs five draw calls

title: The globe costs five draw calls
excerpt: Sixteen pins, labels, a panel and arcs added no draw calls to the globe. The numbers, the test setup, and what they do and do not prove. Plus the same question asked of the city maps.

children.text: The globe page must run on a phone. The repository has a phone probe, and its first commit says it was written before the move from five places to sixteen. That way each change could be measured against a baseline.
The tiers
src/tier.js
picks one of three tiers: full, lite, or static. Phones always get lite. The place cards are plain HTML, so they also work with script off or without WebGL.
The probe
The script
scripts/perf-globe.mjs

runs against a preview build. It uses a 390 by 844 viewport at a pixel ratio of 3, on the lite tier. It slows the CPU four times through the browser's debugging protocol. It then scrolls 180 steps from the top of the page to the end of the globe story. Each result comes from three runs. It records the time between animation frames, the draw calls at the end view, and the triangle count.
The numbers
On the build with five places, the mean frame interval was 18.5 ms in run 1 and 19.1 ms in run 2. The 95th percentile was 33.3 ms and 16.7 ms.
On the build with sixteen places, the mean was 16.7 and 16.8 ms, and the 95th percentile 16.8 ms in both runs. With Lisboa focused, so the panel and arcs were on screen, the mean stayed at 16.7 ms.
The draw calls stayed at 5 in every row. The triangle count stayed at 5,440.
Why the cost did not grow

The pins, the labels, the panel, and the arcs are DOM and SVG elements laid over the canvas. They are not part of the 3D scene. Label placement runs once per drawn frame, for sixteen points. That is a small amount of arithmetic.
As a result, adding a place adds an element in the page, not a mesh in the scene.
What the numbers do not prove

I measured on 14 November on an Apple-silicon Mac using the Metal graphics API. The CPU slowdown is a stress test. The result shows relative cost between builds. It does not show how a real phone behaves.
My own claims list says that no city map has had a test on a real phone. I have no record of a real-phone test for the globe either.
The frame interval of 16.7 ms is the refresh rate of a 60 Hz display. Once a build sits at the refresh rate, the probe cannot show an improvement. It can only show a regression.
The same question for the city maps
On 17 November I asked for the same discipline in the city maps: do not draw the whole map, draw what is visible, and load and unload objects.

The first result came on Porto. Roads are now drawn by the cells in view. A deep link that opens a route improved from 22.7 seconds to 4.8 seconds in a headless run. Desktop frame time and map load time did not change.
I report both parts. The deep link got much faster. The two numbers I hoped to move stayed where they were. An earlier round on Porto cut draw calls from 499 to 281 at the same image.

labels that do not collide

title: What my Claude sessions show about my own work
excerpt: I asked Claude to read the logs of my own sessions on the portugal-3d project. Twenty clean reviews, five usage resets, two false "done" reports, and what logs can never tell you.

children.text: Claude Code writes every session to a log on my machine. The logs are JSON lines. I asked Claude to read the ones for portugal-3d and tell me what they show about my own work.
I limited the read. Claude read my messages and the structured results of reviews. It did not read tool output, because tool output can hold secrets.
Finding 1: the project folder is all reviews

The project folder for portugal-3d holds 20 sessions. Ten run on 7 November and ten on 13 November. All 20 are automated security reviews. Each one received a diff and returned a structured result. All 20 returned an empty list of findings.
They covered the globe, the border, the scroll, the dive and the return, the opener, and the story chapters.
An empty list is a result, not a proof. A reviewer saw only the diff, not the whole repository. And a model wrote each review. What the logs do give me is a record that every change got a look.
Finding 2: my own building happened elsewhere
My conversations about the globe are not in that folder. They sit in one long session in my main folder that began on 28 September. It holds about 230 of my own messages across seven weeks.
The log tells me what I asked and when. It does not hold the reasons. The reasons are in the notes that the session wrote for itself.
Finding 3: usage limits set the rhythm
From 9 October on, the log shows five usage-limit resets, each followed by a message that tells the agent to continue. It shows cut-offs at 01:39 on 14 November and 03:52 on 17 November.
Work does not stop cleanly at these points. This is why my briefs say "commit after each round".
Finding 4: two false "done" reports
A stop hook called done-check compares a completion report with the repository. It flagged two reports in these logs.

On 13 November, it flagged a report that claimed completion. The diff against the main branch touched 81 files and 6,709 added lines. On 15 November, it flagged a report of "merged, pushed and ready" while the working tree was dirty.
The hook caught both, not me.
Finding 5: forty minutes of waiting for a report

On 3 November I sent the same message, "I am waiting for the report, then deploy", 17 times in 39 minutes. In the middle of that I told the agents to stop the hung ones and restart the work step by step.
The problem was the channel, not the wait. If a report does not come, ask why the channel is silent. Do not send the same message again.
Finding 6: two mistakes in the briefs
One agent was briefed with the wrong place. My Pena Park project is in Ribeira de Pena. It is not the Parque da Pena in Sintra. The notes now say so at the top.
Another agent put my email address into the user-agent header of requests to a public map service. My briefs now forbid it.
In both cases the fix went into the brief.
What logs cannot tell you
They cannot show whether a map is good. They cannot show whether a visitor understood a page. They cannot show what a real phone does. They record the process, not the outcome.

title: Elephant, goldfish, me: reviewing a spec with fresh eyes
excerpt: The Elephant-Goldfish Model gives the author a full memory and the reviewers none. How the method works, and what a real run found in an onboarding guide.

children.text: The author of a document knows too much to review it. Every gap in the text fills itself from memory. The author reads what they meant, not what they wrote.
The Elephant-Goldfish Model, EGM, treats that as a design problem. It comes from Google's open-source
elephant-goldfish-model

project. Its docs credit Dave Rensin's article "Elephants, Goldfish, and the New Golden Age of Software Engineering" as the base, and describe EGM as an implementation of spec-driven development. I have the plugin installed in Claude Code. This article covers the method and the one run I can report.
Three roles
The README gives the split in one table.
The
Elephant
holds your project, your requirements, and your earlier decisions. It explores the problem and drafts the specification.
The
Goldfish
reviewers get the document and the source material it references. They do not get the earlier conversation. Their job is to find missing assumptions, unclear requirements, and implementation risks.
You
resolve the trade-offs, approve the design, and decide what to build.
A goldfish forgets, and here that is the feature. A reviewer who has never heard your reasoning cannot fill the gaps with it.
The skills
The plugin ships seven skills. Four of them make the core loop:
/egm-brainstorm
clarifies the idea with you, runs fresh reviewers against it, and saves a
concepts_brief.md
/egm-draft
turns the brief into a design document, one section at a time, and pauses after each section for your feedback.
/egm-review
sends the draft to fresh reviewers in a zero-context session.
/egm-drift-report
compares the documents in a folder with the current source code and reports where they diverge.
The docs also list
egm-bootstrap
egm-resolve
, and
egm-review-loop
. The loop skill lets you pick your own reviewers and standards for documents that are not software specs.

The reviewers are personas, each a separate file. The names include a hostile design critic, a naive reader with zero institutional knowledge, a pedantic checker of documentation against the code, a copy editor, a structural validator, a pragmatic tech lead who checks that a plan leaves no design decisions to the implementer, and a "zoom out" reviewer. A synthesizer merges and deduplicates what they find.

Two lines in the docs matter to me. The review gives "a lot of feedback by design", and you take what is relevant and ignore the rest. And a human review of the design still comes before implementation. EGM does not replace it.
One real run

On 17 November I ran a review on an onboarding guide for a team codebase. The target was one Markdown file of 87 lines. The reviewers worked in stages, and a later stage merged and deduplicated the earlier findings into twelve items.
The final report sorted them like this:
11 proposed fixes, applied.
1 escalated to me.
0 contested, 0 declined.
Three of the findings show how the method works.
A dead remote.

The guide sent iOS work to a repository that was a stale export with a foreign remote. It also named a clone that does not exist on disk. The report rated it a blocker, with the reason "a new engineer would commit to a dead remote". The Elephant, the session with the project context, checked the disk and the project's context files beyond what the reviewers read. The fix followed from those.
A wrong claim in the text.
One section proposed an umbrella repository that "pins branches". Submodules pin commits. The same section was a speculative proposal that nobody had pushed. The fix was to delete it.
Whose numbers.
One person's 30-day usage stats led the guide under the heading "team". The report said the stats tell a newcomer nothing they can act on.

The escalated item shows the third role. A repository was missing from the workspace list, and the reviewers could not tell if that was a mistake. It was my call to make, not theirs. I said the omission was deliberate, because that repository is locked down. The fact then went into the guide as a note.
The guide ended at 79 lines, down from 87.

One more detail from the report. Its first draft gave the new length as 70 lines. That number was wrong, and the report was corrected. A review that checks documents should be able to catch its own figures.
Where it fits in my other spec work

My own checks in the city map repos test a build: the verify command, the fit checks, the evaluator rubric. EGM tests a document before anything is built. The two catch different mistakes. A verify gate cannot see a guide that points to a repository that does not exist. A document review cannot see a model that fails the fit check.
What I have not measured

I have one run. I do not know how many of the twelve findings I would have found by reading the guide again myself. I would need several runs, with a count of accepted findings each time, to say more.

ea
and
cs
slots. This post is for developers who export slides to
.pptx

presentation-md

title: MQTT topics, QoS levels, retained messages and Last Will: what the spec says and where brokers differ
excerpt: A reading of the OASIS MQTT 3.1.1 and 5.0 specs on topics, QoS 0 to 2, retained messages and the Will Message, set next to what Mosquitto and Azure IoT Hub document. Ends with a checklist for an online/offline status topic.

children.text: If a device publishes its status over MQTT, will a new subscriber see it, and will anyone learn when the device drops off the network? This post is for developers who start with MQTT on devices. You get what the spec says about topics, QoS, retained messages and the Will Message, where Mosquitto and Azure IoT Hub document different behaviour, and a checklist for a status topic.
The facts come from the
MQTT 5.0 OASIS Standard
of 7 March 2019 and the
MQTT 3.1.1 OASIS Standard
of 29 October 2014. MQTT 5.0 supersedes 3.1.1. Product behaviour comes from the
Mosquitto configuration manual
, version not stated, read 23 November 2026, and the
Azure IoT Hub MQTT page
, dated 16 November 2026. That page says IoT Hub with the classic connection profile is not a full-featured MQTT broker.
Topics: levels, wildcards and the
prefix
A client publishes to a Topic Name. A subscriber gives a Topic Filter. The
character splits a topic into levels. Topic Names and Topic Filters are case sensitive, so
ACCOUNTS
and
Accounts
are two topics.
Only filters can hold wildcards. The
wildcard matches one level and must fill the whole level. The
wildcard matches the parent level and any number of child levels. It must come last in the filter. A filter that starts with
or
does not match topics that start with
. Mosquitto updates its
$SYS
topics every 10 seconds by default, and
sys_interval 0
turns them off.
QoS 0, 1 and 2: what each level promises

The spec defines three levels. QoS 0 is "at most once": there is no acknowledgement and no retry, so a message can be lost. QoS 1 is "at least once": the receiver answers with PUBACK, and duplicates can arrive. QoS 2 is "exactly once": a four-step flow runs PUBLISH, PUBREC, PUBREL and PUBCOMP.
A subscription carries a maximum QoS. The server delivers at the lower of the published QoS and the granted QoS.
Mosquitto has a
max_qos

option per listener, with a default of 2. A client that publishes above it gets disconnected. Azure IoT Hub, in its classic profile, does not support QoS 2. A device that publishes at QoS 2 loses its connection. A device that subscribes at QoS 2 gets a grant of QoS 1.
Retained messages: the last value on a topic

A PUBLISH with the RETAIN flag set to 1 tells the server to store the message. It replaces the earlier retained message for that topic. A retained message with a zero-byte payload removes the stored one. By default, a new subscriber receives the last retained message on each matching topic.

In MQTT 5.0, Retain Handling 0 sends retained messages on each subscribe, 1 sends them only for a new subscription, and 2 sends none. A Message Expiry Interval can discard a retained message when it runs out.
Mosquitto has
retain_available
, true by default. When it is false, a client that sends a retained message gets disconnected. Azure IoT Hub classic does not store retained messages. It adds an
mqtt-retain
property and passes the message to the backend.
The Will Message: news of an unclean disconnect

A client can put a Will Message in its CONNECT packet. The server publishes it when the network connection closes without a normal DISCONNECT, for example after a missed keep-alive. In 5.0, a DISCONNECT with reason code 0x00 removes the Will Message unsent. In 3.1.1, any DISCONNECT removes it.

MQTT 5.0 adds a Will Delay Interval, 0 by default. The server waits for the interval or for the session end. If the client reconnects first, the server does not send the will. 3.1.1 defines no such interval. With Will Retain set, the server publishes the will as a retained message.
Azure IoT Hub classic tells devices to use its telemetry topics as the will topic. It forwards the will as telemetry, marked with
iothub-MessageType
set to
Will
Checklist: an online/offline status topic
HiveMQ
, a broker vendor, describes a pattern in a February 2026 article. It is vendor guidance, not part of the spec. The checklist adds steps from the spec and product docs:
At CONNECT, set a will of
offline
on a topic such as
client1/status
, with Will Retain on.
After CONNECT, publish a retained
online
to the same topic.
Before a planned DISCONNECT, publish a retained
offline
yourself. A normal DISCONNECT deletes the will, so the topic would still say
online
On MQTT 5.0, decide on a Will Delay Interval. A short reconnect inside the interval sends no
offline
On Azure IoT Hub classic this pattern does not apply. The hub accepts only its own predefined topics, does not store retained messages, and does not support device-to-device communication.
Check if retained messages must survive a broker restart. On Mosquitto, turn on persistence: the built-in
persistence true
or, as the manual recommends, a persistence plugin. Its
autosave_on_changes
entry counts retained messages received toward a save of the built-in database.
HiveMQ's article does not mention step 3. One question stays open. With persistence on, a retained
online
can outlive a broker restart. The 3.1.1 spec lets a server defer the will after its own failure. The sources do not say when Mosquitto then sends it, so a subscriber could read a stale
online
What I could not confirm
The
AWS IoT Core MQTT page
says AWS has "some differences" from the specs. The page was too long to read in full, so this post gives no AWS details.
I did not read sections 4.3 and 4.7 of the 5.0 spec in full. The QoS flow and topic rules come from the 3.1.1 text and the 5.0 packet sections.
No broker was run, so step 6 is not tested.
How this post was made: an AI agent researched and drafted it from the sources linked above, a second agent checked it against those sources, and Timur merged it.

title: What a delta contract shows about the Arouca 3D map and the Braga engine
excerpt: The Arouca 3D map was forked from porto-3d, took its Layers panel from braga-3d, and only then got a written comparison against Braga. Here is the timeline, what the comparison records, and what it leaves open.

children.text: When a 3D map is forked from one engine and later takes code from another, how do you know what it still shares with the engine it borrowed from? This post is for developers who keep several forks of one engine. It follows
arouca-3d
, an interactive 3D map of Arouca, Portugal. The repo's delta contract against braga-3d gives the answer: 15 files are identical to Braga, 88 shared files differ, and 62 files exist only in Braga.
The first commit forks porto-3d at
, and the contract warns that "a large part of the 'changed' list below is engine lineage drift".
The facts come from the repo's
README.md
claude-progress.md
EGM.md
and git log, and the braga-3d git log.
The timeline: fork, port, then contract
The repo has 204 commits, from 2026-10-26 to 2026-11-22.
b2febfb
: "W0 skeleton, fork of porto-3d 4996c26 with Arouca config and 20 seed places".
c1bc8bc
: "Layers: definitions, manifest and status logic with tests (ported from braga-3d)".
dda1978
merges the branch: "Layers panel, loading status and Retry; phones start on Compact".

The progress log lists six files ported from braga-3d:
src/layer-defs.js
src/layers.js

src/load-status.js
scripts/layers-manifest.mjs
and

. The port also added engine hooks in

and

Arouca has three optional layers: the ring tiles around the centre (up to 464 KB), extra buildings (up to 365 KB) and aircraft (14 KB plus live data). The panel offers Light, Compact and Full. Compact is the extra buildings only.

On 2026-11-18 the owner decided that phones of class S and P start on Compact, not on Light. The lite scene (class P) builds no ring, no extra buildings and no life. So class P gets no panel and no status pill.
The checks, and three faults in the first draft

check-layers
: five runs in a row, 41 of 41 at 1440x900 and 42 of 42 at 360x740.

The progress log lists three faults in the first draft of the check and marks them "fixed". No file says whether the fixes came before the five runs. The first draft demanded trail ribbons on a device class that builds none. It read the Retry button one round trip too late, when the pill had gone back to loading. What the delta contract records

compares the fork at
dda1978
with braga-3d at

and

The contract's overview calls the repo "a single-city fork of the Braga 3D engine". Ten lines later it says: "The fork was not cut from Braga. It was cut from porto-3d at

porto-fx
and

For Braga's several city maps on one engine, see
One engine, many cities
What the contract leaves open
The contract names these limits:
In the table of changed files, 70 rows say "Not read": a line count with no inspection of the diff.
"Which side is newer for a given shared file is not determined, except where Braga has files the fork lacks."

For the 62 Braga-only files, "Whether the fork needs each one is not determined." They include walk, game and quest modes, discovery, events and news. They also include 31 files the contract calls landmark models, plus
index.guimaraes.js
. The contract calls these "Braga content".
AGENTS.md
"still says 'W0 skeleton'; it is stale against the git log."
The progress log lists what the Layers work did not test:
No one measured load time on a throttled phone.
No one ran a negative control for the ring-off step.
No one checked physical phones, Safari or Firefox.
The log also notes one bug it did not fix. On a phone with every layer on, the loading pill covers the start marker of an open trail while the area loads.
What is not measured
No file shows a load time for the Layers panel or the Compact preset on a real phone.
The changed-files table has 87 rows. The contract text says 88 shared files differ. No file explains the difference.
The contract counts "31 files" of landmark models but names 30 landmarks. Its Braga-only groups add up to 63 files with 31 models, and to 62 with the 30 names it lists.
No file compares the fork with porto-3d after

title: How ai-usage-meter reads AI tool telemetry switches, then turns them off with a diff and a backup
excerpt: The privacy feature in ai-usage-meter started as a read-only check of telemetry switches for Claude Code and Codex. A second commit added OpenCode and Gemini CLI, and a later commit added a dry-run diff, a backup and a confirm step. Here is what it changes, how it guards config files, and what one measured traffic run showed.

children.text: Which telemetry switches are on for your AI coding tools, and how do you turn them off without damaging their config files? This post is for developers who use Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode or Gemini CLI. It follows the privacy feature of
ai-usage-meter

, a macOS menu-bar app that shows what AI coding tools cost and how much of a plan limit you have used. You get the commands, the exact switches they change, the guards around each file write, and the results of one measured traffic run.
When the privacy feature landed in the repo
The repo has 36 commits, from 2026-11-13 to 2026-11-22, and five tags:
and
. The privacy work is four commits on 2026-11-22. Oldest first:
: "aium privacy, a read-only check of telemetry and feedback switches".
: "OpenCode and Gemini CLI switches".
d0f1e51
: "Privacy section in Settings, backed by aium_privacy".
: "turn off telemetry switches with diff, backup and confirm; measured traffic doc".
The CHANGELOG lists the check, the
--disable
option and the traffic doc under
[Unreleased]
What
aium privacy
reads

body.code: aium privacy                         # which telemetry and feedback switches are set

children.text: The check looks at the process environment and local config files, "and at nothing else". It reports the switches a tool ships, not what the tool sends. Each switch is
Off
Default
(not set, and "for telemetry that default is on") or
On
For Claude Code, it checks five environment switches:
DISABLE_TELEMETRY
DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY
and
CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TELEMETRY
. For Codex, it reads
enabled
under
[analytics]
and
[feedback]
, and whether an
[otel]
section exists. For OpenCode, it reads the
share
setting, the
OPENCODE_DISABLE_SHARE
and
OPENCODE_AUTO_SHARE
environment switches, and
OPENCODE_DISABLE_MODELS_FETCH
. For Gemini CLI, it reads
usageStatisticsEnabled
What
--disable
changes, and what it leaves alone

body.code:
aium privacy --disable               # show the diff, write nothing
aium privacy --disable --yes         # back up each file, then write

children.text: Without
--yes

, the CLI prints the diff and then: "Dry run: nothing was written. Run again with --yes to apply. Each file gets a backup first." When there is nothing to change, it prints this line instead: "Nothing to change: the switches I can set are already off, or the tools are not installed."
--disable
covers three files, and only when the tool's folder exists:
~/.claude/settings.json
: sets
DISABLE_TELEMETRY
DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING
and
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEEDBACK_SURVEY
to
under
env
~/.codex/config.toml
: sets
enabled = false
under
[analytics]
and
[feedback]
~/.gemini/settings.json
: sets
usageStatisticsEnabled
to
false
It does not set
CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC
. A test comment gives the reason: "the switch that also stops updates stays untouched". The module also says: "Nothing here touches a shell profile or a file outside the tools' own config."
How the code guards each config file
plan
only reads.
apply
writes. Before each write,
apply
checks that the file did not change since the plan. If it did, the run stops with "changed since the plan was made. Nothing was written to it. Run again." If the file exists, it copies it to
<name>.aium-backup-<stamp>
. Then it writes the new text to a temporary file and renames that file into place.
The tests in
crates/core/tests/privacy_fix.rs
pin down more cases:
Other keys in Claude settings keep their order and values.
A second run plans no changes.
Codex
[analytics]
with no
enabled
key gets the key inserted.
An inline table such as
analytics = { enabled = true }
, or a settings file that is not valid JSON, is refused and left as it was.
One limit is in the code comments.
apply
"stops at the first problem; files written before it stay written and keep their backups."
What one measured traffic run showed
The commit that added
--disable
also added
docs/what-tools-send.md

. On 2026-11-22, on one Apple Silicon Mac, Claude Code 2.1.330 and Codex 0.170.0 each ran once with the prompt "Reply with the single word ok.". Traffic went through a local mitmproxy. The proxy recorded hosts, paths, header names and JSON key names, not values.
Claude Code sent
POST /api/event_logging/v2/batch
4 times, at about 1 MB and 400 events each. In the first batch, 289 of 400 events were
tengu_skill_loaded
. The doc also lists a
POST
to
http-intake.logs.us5.datadoghq.com
, described as "Logs sent to Datadog".
Codex sent
POST /backend-api/codex/analytics-events/events
6 times. It also sent metrics to
ab.chatgpt.com/otlp/v1/metrics
A credential in a URL path on the first capture

On the first capture attempt, the proxy script kept URL paths whole. One path held a credential that a plugin puts in the URL. The script now masks path segments that are not short and plain. The doc's advice: if you repeat this, mask paths from the start.
What is not measured
No capture ran with the switches set. The doc says "A second capture with the switches set would test them." So the repo does not show which requests each switch stops.
The capture did not record values. It does not show whether
skill_name
is a plain name or a hash, or how much of each 400-event batch was a backlog from earlier sessions.
OpenCode and Gemini CLI traffic was not captured. Only their switches were read.
The capture covers one Mac, one day, one short run, and one version of each tool.
This post does not report a test run. No file read for it shows test results.

title: Sip, a SwiftUI water tracker: Live Activity, Apple Health sync without duplicates, and what the tests cover
excerpt: How a SwiftUI water tracker writes drinks to Apple Health so that edits replace a sample and deletes remove it, how its Live Activity starts, updates and ends, how tea and coffee count toward the goal, and which parts the tests reach and which they do not.

children.text: How do you write drinks to Apple Health so that an edit replaces a sample and does not add a second one? Short answer: give each sample the drink's UUID as its HealthKit sync identifier, and save an edit with a higher sync version, so HealthKit replaces the old sample.
This post is for iOS developers who build a small logging app with HealthKit, ActivityKit and widgets. It follows Sip, a SwiftUI water tracker in the
sim-pane-demo
repo. You also get the Live Activity rules, the hydration factors, and what the tests cover and leave out.
When each feature landed in the repo
The repo has 26 commits, from 2026-11-18 to 2026-11-24. The first commit,
ab90ebf
, is "Sip: SwiftUI water tracker with 3D glass, onboarding, history, settings, UI tests". On 2026-11-23, three commits added the features in this post, oldest first:
: "Hydration factors (tea 90%, coffee 80%), shown per drink, switch in Settings".
: "Apple Health: write drinks as Water with sync identifiers (edits replace, deletes remove)".
fb2cf09
: "Live Activity: Lock Screen card and Dynamic Island with one-tap logging; ends an hour after goal or at midnight".
A later commit that day,
42e33af
, added a "Live Activity quick-add UI test".
How Apple Health sync avoids duplicates
HealthSync

saves each drink as one Dietary Water sample. The sample's HealthKit sync identifier is the drink's UUID. The code comment says: "Saving again with a higher sync version replaces the old sample (HealthKit does this), so edits never duplicate."
A small ledger remembers what Sip last wrote. For each drink, it stores a fingerprint (the counted amount, the time in whole seconds, and the kind) and a version. The
plan
function compares drinks to the ledger:
A new drink gets version 1.
A drink whose fingerprint changed gets the next version, with the same sync identifier.
A drink that is gone from the log gets deleted from Health by its sync identifier.
A drink older than 30 days leaves the ledger. The test says "history stays in Health".

Two details came from things that can go wrong. First, a comment says turning Health off keeps the ledger: "HealthKit ignores a sync version that is not higher than the stored one, so restarting versions at 1 would silently drop updates." Second, drink times are whole seconds. The JSON log stores seconds, so "a sub-second time would not survive a save and reload, and an untouched drink would compare as changed."
How tea and coffee count toward the goal
DrinkKind

gives each kind a factor: water 1.0, tea 0.9, coffee 0.8, sparkling 1.0, and an unknown kind counts as 1. A switch in Settings turns the factors off, and then each drink counts in full. The source comment says the factors "follow common hydration-index findings". The source file cites no study.

The factor also reaches Health, because Sip writes the counted amount. A unit test turns the switch off for a 250 ml coffee. The plan then saves version 2 of that sample: "250 counted instead of 200, so the sample is replaced".
How the Live Activity starts, updates and ends
LiveProgress.sync
keeps one Live Activity in step with the day's total. If the switch is off, or the system does not allow Live Activities, it calls
endAll()
Otherwise it takes one of four branches:
An activity is live and the goal is not reached: it updates the activity.
An activity is live and the goal is reached: it ends the activity with a dismissal one hour later.
No activity is live and the goal is not reached: it starts one.
No activity is live and the goal is reached: it does nothing.
A comment records a trap: "Ended activities stay in
activities
for a while, so filter by state: updating an ended activity does nothing and would block a new day's activity." So
current
counts only activities that are active or stale. The test asserts "an ended activity must not count as current".
What the tests cover
A search of the three test folders finds 62
func test
declarations: 45 in
Tests
, 14 in
UITests
and 3 in
WatchUITests
HealthPlanTests

checks the no-duplicates rules "without touching HealthKit". It covers version 1 for new drinks, no writes on a second run, a version bump on edit, a delete, the 30-day age-out, and the hydration switch.
testHealthSyncHasNoDuplicates

is a UI test with "Real HealthKit on the simulator". It logs two drinks, turns on the Health switch, and expects "2 drinks" in Settings. After an edit it expects "2 drinks" again (failure message: "edit duplicated"). After a delete it expects "1 drink" ("delete left a sample").
LiveProgressTests
checks the percent math and the end date. One test runs "Real ActivityKit in the simulator": switch on, log, switch off. It skips when Live Activities are off in that simulator.
SipLiveActivityTests
opens Notification Center, taps "+250 ml" on the Live Activity, and checks that the total on the Today screen changes. It waits three seconds with
sleep(3)
while the intent runs.
scripts/flaky.sh
runs one UI test up to N times (4 by default) and prints the failure messages on the first failure.
What broke on the way to the App Store
Commit
5aaf00a

on 2026-11-24 starts with: "App Store: iPhone-only build (Apple rejected portrait-only iPad)". The listing doc now sets the devices to "iPhone only (TARGETED_DEVICE_FAMILY 1), plus the watch app". The repo does not show whether the new build passed review.
What is not measured
No file shows a test run result. This post reports test names and assertions, not pass rates.
The
HealthSync.sync
path that calls HealthKit has no unit test. One simulator UI test checks it through the Settings read-back count.
The roadmap says the Health device build "needs a signing team". Commit
17c2c4c
on 2026-11-24 set up App Store signing. No file shows the Health sync run on a real device.
No test reads the Dynamic Island. The Live Activity UI test uses Notification Center.
No file gives a flake rate for the UI tests.

title: How the Pena Park 3D tour handles 29 languages and checks its translations
excerpt: A Three.js scroll tour lists 29 languages in its menu. Two are written in the code, 27 come from JSON files. Here is how the app picks a language, falls back to English, and how one script fails a translation that loses a number.

children.text: How do you ship a small 3D site in 29 languages when no native speaker has read 27 of them? This post is for developers who add translations to a static web app. It follows
pena-park-3d

, a real-scale Three.js map of Pena Park Hotel and Pena Aventura Park in Ribeira de Pena, Portugal. The repo calls it an "unofficial concept demo". You get the file layout, the fallback rules, and the checks one script runs on each translation file.
What the git history can and cannot show
The repo has one commit:

on 2026-11-22, "Initial commit: Pena Park 3D as it stands on 2026-11-22". So git gives no order of events for the language work. The README says the site went public at https://pena-park-3d.vercel.app on 2026-10-31.
Two languages in the code, 27 in files
LANGS
in
src/i18n.js
lists 29 languages. English and Portuguese are written in the code. The chapter copy lives in
src/journey.js
, the figures in
data/facts.json
, and the UI strings in
STRINGS
in
src/ui.js
Every other language comes from
data/i18n/<code>.json
. The manifest
data/i18n/index.json
lists 27 files, from
es.json
to
th.json
. The English source file
_source.en.json
holds 281 keys.
Keys are stable paths, for example
chapter.<id>.title
or
fact.<id>.value
. The app and the extract script build them from the same object
K
. A code comment says this is so "the two can never disagree".
How the app picks a language
resolveLang
tries four sources in order:
?lang=
in the URL, then
localStorage.lang
, then the browser languages, then English. A source that names no known language falls through to the next one.
matchLang
maps tags to the registry.
pt-BR
becomes
pt
zh-TW
zh-HK
and
zh-MO
become
zh-Hant
, and other
zh
becomes
zh-Hans
nb
and
nn
become
no
, and the old code
iw
becomes
he
How English fills the gaps
The app fetches
index.json
first, so it does not ask for a file that the manifest does not list. A missing key, a missing file or a failed fetch falls back to English, string by string. A string that falls back carries
lang="en"
When two language switches overlap, a counter makes the later call win over a slower earlier one.
Right-to-left and script fonts
Arabic and Hebrew set
dir="rtl"
on the page. The app also sets
data-script
, and
src/style.css
gives each script its own system font stack. The app downloads no web fonts.
One bidi problem has its own fix. A code comment says that in an rtl page, European digits after Arabic letters turn into Arabic numbers, so "2026-10-29" shows as "29-10-2026".
bidiSafe
wraps each ISO date in left-to-right isolate marks when the page is rtl.
The check that fails a translation
The workflow in the README has five steps:

body.code:
node scripts/i18n-extract.mjs
# translate data/i18n/_source.en.json, read each _note
# save it as data/i18n/<code>.json
node scripts/i18n-check.mjs
# list the file in data/i18n/index.json

children.text: scripts/i18n-check.mjs
exits with 1 on any FAIL. Its header lists these FAIL rules for a translation file:
invalid JSON, a missing key, an extra key, or an empty string;
_meta.lang
that is not the file's code;
a lost number: each run of digits in the English must appear as many times in the translation ("8.08" may become "8,08");
a lost URL, ISO date,
{placeholder}
, "©" or "ODbL";
a
{placeholder}
that the English does not have;
placeholder text such as TODO or "lorem ipsum".
The whole run also fails when
_source.en.json
is stale, or when
index.json
lists a file that does not exist.
The script warns, and does not fail, for:
a length ratio outside 0.4 to 3.5, for English strings of 8 or more characters;
a missing protected name such as "Fantasticable" or "Caminho do Abade";
a
_meta.sourceHash
that differs from the current source;
a language file that
index.json
does not list.
npm run verify
runs this check as step (i). For more on checks of this kind, see
Requirements a machine can check
For each file the script prints one summary line in this format (source code, not a captured run):

body.code: <PASS or FAIL>  <file>: <n>/<total> keys, <n> identical to English (names and figures), <n> lost numbers, <n> warnings

children.text: The first word is FAIL when a key is missing, a string is empty, a string lost a number or token, or a string holds an unknown placeholder or placeholder text. An extra key or a wrong
_meta.lang
prints its own FAIL line, but the summary line can still read PASS. Either way the run exits with 1. A file with invalid JSON or no
strings
object gets no summary line.
scripts/build-public.mjs
copies
data/i18n/
into the public build, but skips names that start with
. So the translator input
_source.en.json
stays out of
dist/
Who wrote the translations
The README says all 27 translated files are machine translations (Claude), "checked for keys and figures but not read by a native speaker". In the
_meta
blocks, 26 of the 27 files read
"translator": "machine (Claude), unreviewed"
es.json
reads
"translator": "pilot translation (agent), from _source.en.json"
What is not measured
No file in the repo shows a captured output of
node scripts/i18n-check.mjs
or
npm run verify
. This post does not claim a pass.
No native speaker has read the 27 translated files, per the README. Their quality is unknown.
The check counts digits, tokens and keys. It does not test meaning, tone, or grammar.
No screenshot in the sources shows the rtl layout or the script fonts on a real device.
How this post was made: an AI agent drafted it from the project files listed in the repo, a second agent reviewed it, and Timur merged it.

title: life-mcp: the tool schema and guards of a workout and meal tracker that AI assistants write to
excerpt: life-mcp is a small MCP server on a Cloudflare Worker with Neon Postgres. An assistant turns plain talk about meals and training into rows. Here are its three tables, its eight tools, the instructions it sends on connect, the guards on SQL and edits, and what the repo does not test.

children.text: How do you let an AI assistant write your meals and workouts into a database without giving it write access to the whole database? This post is for developers who want to build a small remote MCP server for personal data. It follows
life-mcp
, a Cloudflare Worker with Neon Postgres.
The short answer from its code: writes go through fixed tools, and
update_row
changes only columns on a fixed list per table. Free SQL runs in a
READ ONLY
transaction. But reads are not limited to the three tables: a
SELECT
can read any table the database user can read. You also get the tables, the tool schema and the instructions the server sends to the model.
What the git history shows
The repo has 3 commits, all on 2026-11-23. Oldest first:
fd497bd
: "Life MCP: Cloudflare Worker with Neon Postgres, MCP and REST doors".
7bf1ba3
: "Track fiber: meals.fiber_g column, log_meal, update_row and summary".
adcb4cb
: "Tell the model to estimate fiber too".
The repo has no tags and no README. The main packages in
package.json
are
wrangler
typescript
@neondatabase/serverless
^1.2.1. The Worker sets
compatibility_date
to
Three tables, with dates as plain text
schema.sql
holds three tables:
workouts
meals
and
entries
. Each date is
TEXT
in the form
YYYY-MM-DD
, with a
CHECK
on that pattern. The schema comment gives the reason: "so they travel as plain strings". The schema comment tells readers to cast with
date::date
when they need date math.
workouts
keeps exercises in a
sets
column of type
JSONB
meals
has
calories
protein_g
carbs_g
fat_g
and
fiber_g
entries
covers "Anything else: weight, sleep, mood, supplements" with a
kind
and a
JSONB
data
object.
The
meals
table in
CREATE TABLE
has
fiber_g
. One more line, with its own comment, adds the column to older databases:

body.code:
-- Added 2026-11-23 for databases created before fiber was tracked.
ALTER TABLE meals ADD COLUMN IF NOT EXISTS fiber_g DOUBLE PRECISION;

children.text: Eight tools for writing, reading and fixing rows
src/index.ts
lists eight tools:
log_workout
log_meal
and
add_entry
write one row each.
recent
lists the newest rows of one table. The default limit is 20, and the maximum is 100.
summary
gives meal and workout totals per day, and a count of other entries per kind, for a date range. The default range is the last 7 days.
query
runs one read-only SQL
SELECT
update_row
and
delete_row
change or remove one row by id.
Here is the schema for
log_meal
, as it is in the code:

body.code:
inputSchema: {
  type: "object",
  properties: {
    date: { type: "string", description: "YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today (UTC)." },
    meal: { type: "string", enum: ["breakfast", "lunch", "dinner", "snack"] },
    description: { type: "string" },
    calories: { type: "integer" },
    protein_g: { type: "number" },
    carbs_g: { type: "number" },
    fat_g: { type: "number" },
    fiber_g: { type: "number" },
    notes: { type: "string" },
  },
  required: ["meal", "description"],
},

children.text: Only
meal
and
description
are required. The schema describes the optional
date
field as "YYYY-MM-DD. Defaults to today (UTC)."
The instructions the server sends on connect
The
initialize
reply carries an
instructions

string. The code comment says it "tells the assistant how to turn plain talk into rows". The first line says: "Personal life tracker. The user talks in plain language; you fill the fields. Never ask the user to name tables or fields."
The instructions map talk to tools. Food goes to
log_meal
, training goes to
log_workout
, and the rest goes to
add_entry
. For entries, they give a list of kinds to reuse, such as weight
{kg}
, sleep
{hours, quality_1_5}
and water
{ml}
The food line says: "Estimate calories, protein_g, carbs_g, fat_g and fiber_g when the user gives none, and say they are estimates." This post does not show what commit
adcb4cb
changed in that line.
The instructions tell the model to ask the user a question "only when a missing detail changes the record a lot". Before
update_row
or
delete_row
, they tell it to find the row id and confirm "when more than one row could match".
Guards on SQL, edits and access
The
query
tool takes free SQL, so it has the most guards:
The text must start with
select
or
with
A
inside the text is refused: "Send one statement only."
The query runs in a
READ ONLY
transaction with
SET LOCAL statement_timeout = '5s'
The reply holds at most 500 rows.
The guard does not check table names.
update_row
changes only columns on a fixed list per table. Other names get the error "Cannot change: ...", with the allowed list.
id
accepts digit strings too, because "Postgres returns bigint ids as strings".
On the MCP route, the message from these checks goes back as text with
isError: true
. Other errors go back as "The database call failed.", and the code logs the details with
console.error
Access uses a bearer token,
MCP_TOKEN
. A second path,
/mcp/<secret>
, serves "clients that cannot send a header", with its own
MCP_PATH_TOKEN
. The code hashes both values with SHA-256 and compares them with
timingSafeEqual
If
MCP_TOKEN
or
DATABASE_URL
is not set, the MCP and REST routes return 503. The comment says: "The secret is the only protection".
One tool set, two ways in
The Worker speaks "Stateless Streamable HTTP: one JSON-RPC request in, one JSON response out". It lists protocol versions
and
. When a client asks for another version,
initialize
answers with
A second route,
POST /api/tools/<tool>
, is the "REST door for the native app". It calls the same
callTool
function, so the checks inside the tools apply on both routes. The REST route takes only the bearer
MCP_TOKEN
, not the path secret. A check error there returns status 400, and other errors return 500.
What is not measured
The repo has no tests. The
test
script prints "Error: no test specified". A
typecheck
script exists, but no file shows its result.
No file shows latency, row counts, or how often the model estimates nutrition correctly.
The native app that uses the REST door is not in the repo.
Dates default to UTC. The repo does not show what happens to a meal logged near midnight in another time zone.
No file shows a test of the
query
guards against SQL that tries to write.
How this post was made: an AI agent drafted it from the repo's `src/index.ts`, `schema.sql`, `package.json`, `wrangler.jsonc` and git history, a second agent reviewed it, and Timur merged it.

title: Haru-4B on an M1 Max: how much of its 133 ms frame the MLX build uses
excerpt: Haru-4B is a full-duplex speech model that must finish one step every 133 ms. On an M1 Max laptop, the repo's MLX test notes record 43 ms per frame in bfloat16 and 31 ms in 8-bit, about a third and a quarter of the frame. Here is how to run a similar measurement, the numbers, where they disagree, and what the files do not measure.

children.text: Can a full-duplex speech model keep up with real time on an M1 Max laptop? This post is for developers who want to run
Haru-4B
on an Apple silicon Mac. You get the frame budget, the per-frame times that the files record on an M1 Max, how to run a similar measurement, and the gaps in those numbers.

The short answer from the files: the recorded per-frame times are well under 133 ms, but no file shows the slowest frame or the timing of a live run. One frame holds 133 ms of audio. The MLX test notes record 31 ms per frame with
--quantize 8
and 43 ms in bfloat16, from a run of
python -m haru_mlx.run_inference
on a 31 s recording. They do not name the statistic.

A local research report, citing the developer blog, gives a model step of 34.2 ms in int8. The 31 ms and 34.2 ms figures are each about a quarter of the frame. The files do not say which build gave the blog figure, or whether the two figures cover the same work.
What Haru-4B does in one frame

Haru listens and speaks at the same time. The README says: "Every 133 ms the model takes one frame of the user's audio and produces one frame of its own audio and text." That is a rate of 7.5 Hz. User audio, model audio and model text are summed into one position of the language model.
So the deadline is fixed. To keep up in real time, each step has to finish inside the 133 ms frame.
What the git history shows
The repo has one commit:
7fe6b76
, dated 2026-11-13, "Release haru-speech and haru-speech-vllm 0.1.1". It has two tags:
haru-speech-v0.1.1
and
haru-speech-vllm-v0.1.1
. The history does not show how the code got to that state. The MLX build for Apple silicon lives in
haru_mlx/
How to run a similar measurement
The test notes name the script,
python -m haru_mlx.run_inference
, the
--quantize 8
flag and "a 31 s recording". They do not give the exact arguments of their run: no input file, reference clip or system prompt. The commands below follow the generic example in the MLX README.
The MLX package installs from its own folder. The checkpoint is about 10 GB and downloads from Hugging Face on first use.

body.code:
cd haru_mlx
pip install -e .
python -m haru_mlx.run_inference user.wav reply.wav --reference voice.wav --system-prompt "..."
python -m haru_mlx.run_inference user.wav reply.wav --reference voice.wav --system-prompt "..." --quantize 8

children.text: The script prints a summary line, then the transcript. This is the format string of the summary line in
run_inference.py

body.code: print(f"{count} frames ({count * frame_samples / SAMPLE_RATE:.1f} s), {step_ms:.1f} ms per frame -> {args.output}")

children.text: The
step_ms
value is the median time of every frame after the first one, which comes from
session.start()
. The test notes do not say that their figures quote this printed line.
The numbers on an M1 Max
The test notes name the machine: a MacBook Pro with an M1 Max chip, 64 GB, macOS 26.6, MLX 0.32.4. On a 31 s recording, the run took:
--quantize none
(bfloat16): 43 ms per frame, 13.5 GB peak memory.
--quantize 8
: 31 ms per frame, 11.2 GB peak memory.
Against the 133 ms frame, that is about 32% of the budget in bfloat16 and about 23% in 8-bit. These shares are arithmetic. The repo does not state them.
The 8-bit mode quantizes the language model's weight matrices and the embedding table. The audio codec, the audio head and the normalization gains keep the checkpoint's precision.
Three more int8 figures from builds the files do not name

A local research report in Russian, not part of the published repo, compares open full-duplex models. It records an offline run, by the person it was written for, at 47 ms per frame in int8. The files do not say which build, recording or settings gave 47 ms.
The report also cites the
Higurashi technical blog

: p50 of 65.2 ms on an M1 Max with int8 weights, of which the model step is 34.2 ms, so the p50 measures more than the step. The blog's step is 34.2 ms and the test notes' figure is 31 ms per frame. The files do not show whether the two cover the same work:
frame.seconds
in
session.py
spans from the start of
step()
through the backbone, the audio head and the codec decode.
The files do not say what the other ~31 ms of the p50 covers. From the blog numbers and the 47 ms run, the report concludes that Haru spends about a third to a half of its frame budget.

The report adds a cost. A 133 ms frame adds up to 133 ms of framing delay. Moshi-family models use an 80 ms frame. The report says the spare time lowers the risk of falling behind real time, but it does not make Haru's replies faster.
What the research notes record for Moshi-family step times
Moshi and its successor PersonaPlex run at 12.5 Hz, so each step must finish within 80 ms. The research notes collect three PersonaPlex figures on an M2 Max for the community Swift port,
speech-swift
A news write-up
gives about 68 ms per step in 4-bit (RTF 0.87), and the notes call it "Developer-measured, not independent". The port's own README lists "~0.94 RTF on M2 Max".
A search-engine summary of the port's
guide

gives about 112 ms per step in 8-bit (RTF about 1.4), and the notes mark it unverified. The notes flag all three figures as in conflict. The report states that no independent M1 Max numbers exist for these models.
What is not measured

The report mentions a failure: a live test, run by the person the report was written for, broke. The report points at the audio path, not at model speed. It suggests wired headphones and the Mac's built-in microphone in place of Bluetooth and the iPhone microphone through Continuity. No file shows the result of that check.
The repo's 43 ms and 31 ms figures come from one 31 s recording on one M1 Max. The repo's test notes name no other Mac.
No file shows a live-conversation latency from the macOS app.
No Full-Duplex-Bench score for Haru appears in the repo. The report says no independent Full-Duplex-Bench measurement of Haru appeared by 18 November 2026.
No side-by-side run of Haru, Moshi and PersonaPlex on one machine appears.
How this post was made: an AI agent drafted it from the listed sources (the Haru repo plus local research notes), a second agent reviewed it, and Timur merged it.

title: Porto 3D walk mode: four street-level faults and the numbers behind each fix
excerpt: Walk mode came to the porto-3d map on 24 November 2026. In the next two days the progress log records a walk that froze, streets drawn as terraces, a hump of terrain on the Ribeira quay, and paving that disagreed with the ground. Here are the causes, the fixes, the counts, and what is still open.

children.text: What breaks when you walk at eye height through a 3D city map built to be seen from above? This post is for developers who build Three.js maps on terrain and OpenStreetMap (OSM) data. It follows four faults in the
porto-3d
progress log. Each comes with its measured cause, fix commit, counts and open ends.
Where walk mode came from
porto-3d has 166 commits from 2 October to 26 November 2026. Walk mode arrived in
e2efaf7
on 24 November, ported from braga-3d with a GLB walker and a
/play
page.
One engine, many cities
covers the shared engine.
Fault 1: the walk froze every few seconds
The
hitch.mjs
probe on porto-3d.com found long tasks of 0.3 to 0.5 s every 4 to 5 s. A CPU profile put 80 % of that time in
readSurface
in
walk.js
. It re-read all 66 walkable meshes, about 1 M triangles, whenever the set of visible meshes changed.
The fix in

builds the new index as a generator, 3 ms per frame, while the old index stays in use. In two 40 s runs, long tasks over 200 ms fell from 6 and 6 on main to 0 and 1. Start, teleport and a walker near the edge of the old index still read in one go.
Fault 2: sloped streets looked like terraces
At the Ponte Luís I lower deck, the road looked like flat plates at different heights. Two causes:
strip()
in
src/roads.js
drew one quad per 12 m segment, lengthened at both ends, flat at the end height. On a slope, one quad's end lay over the next quad's start, 0.1 to 0.3 m apart.
At the bridge ends, each way gets its ramp from its own junction. Ways that overlap in plan stood 0.3 to 1.4 m apart.
The fix in
mitres the joint at bends up to 60 degrees. In
harmoniseRamps()
, where two ramps overlap in plan and stand less than 3 m apart, the lower takes the higher's lift. Stacked samples on Mouzinho da Silveira fell from 27 of 60 to 1 of 60.
Fault 3: a hump of terrain on the Ribeira quay, then a start in the river

The owner reported "humps of terrain in front of the arcades" at Praça da Ribeira. The DEM, a 25 to 30 m source, smears the quay wall and the hill into one ramp, 10 to 13 m high at the house fronts. The real quay is about 4 to 5 m.
Commit
adds a quay terrace polygon at 4.6 m above sea level. Across the square, the ground went from 2.8–13.9 m to 3.9–4.8 m.
The entry's follow-up records a regression. The default
/play
start stood waist-deep in the river. The start lies 14 m river-ward of the OSM quay line.

"The terrace lifts the ground only to the quay line", so the ground under the deck is the river bed. The deck stood 3 m over it, more than the walker climbs (1.8 m), so it was a ceiling. The start check had passed with the walker in the river.
Commit
pins the deck to the terrace level. In
walk.js
, a quay deck is now a floor wherever it stands over the terrain. The start check now asks that the feet are on the top drawn surface.
Fault 4: paving and ground disagreed in the old centre

Around the Luís I bridge foot, paving lay at odd angles on a raw hillside, and a bench and a parked car floated. One of five measured causes: "the drawn ground is a 12 m lattice: it cannot follow a 6 m street cut into a slope".
Commit
adds
src/street-ground.js

. It builds a 2 m raster from the street network over a 1.15 x 1.14 km district, drawn on a 3 m lattice. The log's metric script measured a smaller box around the bridge foot (41.1395-41.1440, -8.6160 to -8.6080, 1.5 m grid), not the whole district. The counts, main against branch:
Drawn ground over the top paving by more than 0.15 m: 1,105 of 28,297 on main, 44 of 29,883 on the branch.
Props more than 0.2 m off the top drawn surface: 209 of 592 on main, 5 of 611 on the branch.
At the
/play
start, triangles rose by about 6 %.
ready
went from 17.3 s to 18.7 s on a loaded machine. The log records
npm test
npm run verify
OK, 17 passed.
What the log lists as not fixed, and what later entries change
A one-off shader compile when a new material first draws. porto-038 listed it on 25 November. On 26 November, porto-040 added idle-slot material precompiling for the map (
). The log does not record its effect in walk mode.

The bridge-end ramps and the east embankment, which later entries partly close. porto-037 (25 November) listed the ramps at "6 to 9 m over the DEM on grass embankments", and porto-039 (26 November, before the street ground work) called the east embankment "still a dark grass wedge beside the bridge abutment". porto-041 no longer lists them and reports paving on a wall or embankment at 699 -> 113, "now granite walls, no grass embankments", in its metric box around the bridge foot (41.1395-41.1440, -8.6160 to -8.6080). The log does not record the effect on the east embankment itself.
In porto-039, Largo Luiz I on the Gaia side "still stands 9 m over the DEM". The log does not record whether porto-041 changed it.
The 44 remaining ground samples sit where OSM draws ways over each other 2 to 5 m apart.
What is not measured
Frame time on the owner's laptop. For the walk level of detail, the log says it "decides whether stage 1b or 2 is needed".
GPU time, in part. GPU timer queries on the M1 Max were too noisy to report (porto-033). porto-041 gives one paired run: 59.8 ms on main, 59.1 ms on the branch.
The street ground step on a throttled phone CPU: "Not measured apart". The perf soft gate missed 11 budgets at a load average of about 25.
How this post was made: an AI agent drafted it from the project files listed in the repo, a second agent reviewed it, and Timur merged it.
